+| `POST` | `/inventory/{skuId}/purchase` | Deduct stock, only if enough is on hand | `200` JSON, `400` / `404` text | Not started |
+Request bodies are `{"quantity": <integer ≥ 1>}`. Success bodies are
+`{"skuId": "...", "quantity": <integer ≥ 0>}`. Error bodies are plain-text strings
+(`text/plain`), not JSON.
+## Tech stack
+| Choice | Why |
+| **Kotlin** (JVM) | Nuuly's production language, and one I want to learn in depth (see [Learning Kotlin](#learning-kotlin-with-this-project)). |
+| **Spring Boot**, Spring MVC | Nuuly's production framework. Nuuly evaluated Micronaut and found its speed gains didn't outweigh the environment problems it caused, so they chose Spring. |
+| **Gradle, Kotlin DSL** | The standard build for Kotlin and Spring. Build scripts are written in Kotlin too. |
+| **JUnit 5** + Spring test support | Controller tests via `MockMvc`, plus full-context integration tests. |
+Exact versions (Spring Boot, Kotlin, JDK) will be pinned when the project is scaffolded
+and recorded here.
+## Open decisions
+These are settled one at a time before the code that depends on them is written.
+Each decision and its reasoning is recorded here once it is made.
+| Decision | Options under consideration | Status |
+| Data store | **PostgreSQL**, run with Docker Compose. Considered in-memory and H2; see below. | Decided 2026-09-23 |
+| Concurrency on purchase | **Single atomic SQL statements** + `CHECK (quantity >= 0)` backstop. See below. | Decided 2026-09-23 |
+| Data-access library | **`JdbcClient`**: explicit SQL, maps to immutable data classes. Considered Spring Data JDBC, Spring Data JPA, Exposed. | Decided 2026-09-23 |

+| Controllers | **Hand-written**, plus a contract-validation test (responses checked against `inventory.yaml`). Considered generating them with `openapi-generator`, but that hides the Spring MVC wiring and is overkill for 4 endpoints. | Decided 2026-09-23 |

+| Schema migrations | **Flyway**: versioned plain-SQL files, run automatically at startup and in tests. Considered Liquibase (XML/YAML changesets, more ceremony) and `schema.sql` (no versioning). | Decided 2026-09-23 |
+| Contract gaps | Malformed or missing JSON body, `quantity` of wrong type, SKU id format/case sensitivity, integer overflow on add | Open |
+### Decision record: PostgreSQL and atomic SQL
+The key requirement is that **a purchase must never oversell, even when requests arrive at
+the same moment.** In PostgreSQL, each write is a single atomic statement, so the database
+guarantees this without any locking code in the application:
+```sql
+-- Receive stock: create the SKU or add to it
+INSERT INTO inventory (sku_id, quantity) VALUES (?, ?)
+ON CONFLICT (sku_id) DO UPDATE SET quantity = inventory.quantity + EXCLUDED.quantity
+RETURNING sku_id, quantity;
+-- Purchase: succeeds only if enough stock exists (0 rows updated -> 404 or 400)
+UPDATE inventory SET quantity = quantity - ?
+WHERE sku_id = ? AND quantity >= ?
+RETURNING sku_id, quantity;
+There is no read-then-write race, and correctness still holds with several instances of the
+service running. A `CHECK (quantity >= 0)` constraint is a second line of defense.
+Alternatives we rejected:
+- **In-memory map:** needs no setup, but data is lost on restart and it only works with a
+  single instance.
+- **H2:** its SQL dialect differs from production databases.
+- **Redis / document stores:** add nothing for a single integer per key.
+Kotlin doesn't favor any particular database; it uses the same JDBC drivers as Java. It does
+favor data-access libraries that work with immutable `data class`es (`JdbcClient`, Spring Data
+JDBC, Exposed) over JPA, which needs compiler plugins to work around Kotlin's final-by-default classes.
+The oversell guarantee is tested with several different mechanisms: race tests, a negative
+control, multi-instance tests, load tests and property-based tests. The full plan is in
+[.claude/TODO.md](.claude/TODO.md#oversell-protection-test-plan).
+## Build and run
+**Prerequisites:** JDK 21 and Docker Desktop (running). Postgres starts automatically in a
+container; there is nothing to install or configure by hand.
+_Commands coming with the first scaffold commit._ The goal is one command to run and one to test.
+## Project layout
+```text
+.claude/                 Claude Code configuration (hooks, agents, skills) — see below
+CLAUDE.md                Project memory and coding standards for Claude Code
+src/main/resources/
+  openapi/inventory.yaml The OpenAPI contract (source of truth)
+docs/
+  learning/              Kotlin/Spring concept index and walkthrough logs
+  ai-sessions/           Exported transcripts of every AI session on this project
+scripts/                 Hook scripts (branch guard, KDoc check, session export)
+## Learning Kotlin with this project
+I'm using this assessment to learn Kotlin properly, so the code is commented far more
+heavily than normal production code:
+- **KDoc on every non-private declaration**: what it does, why it exists, and where it
+  sits in the request flow.
+- **Tagged inline comments** that can be searched:
+  - `// Kotlin:` explains a language feature, often compared with Java
+  - `// Spring:` explains framework behavior that is otherwise invisible
+  - `// Why:` records a design decision and the alternative that was rejected
+  - `// Contract:` ties a line to a specific rule in the OpenAPI spec
+- **A walkthrough after every feature.** Before moving on, I go through the new code line by
+  line with Claude, answer check-your-understanding questions, and log the session in
+  [docs/learning/walkthroughs/](docs/learning/walkthroughs/). New concepts are indexed in
+  [docs/learning/kotlin-concepts.md](docs/learning/kotlin-concepts.md).
+## AI-assisted development
+I'm building this with [Claude Code](https://claude.com/claude-code). The configuration is
+committed so reviewers can see how the AI was directed and checked:
+| File | Purpose |
+| [CLAUDE.md](CLAUDE.md) | Project memory: contract rules, stack, commenting standard, feature workflow. |
+| [.claude/skills/feature](.claude/skills/feature/SKILL.md) | `/feature`: contract check → approved plan → tests + code → build → doc review → README → walkthrough hand-off. |
+| [.claude/skills/walkthrough](.claude/skills/walkthrough/SKILL.md) | `/walkthrough`: interactive, file-by-file teaching session with understanding checks, logged to `docs/learning/`. |
+| [.claude/skills/ship](.claude/skills/ship/SKILL.md) | `/ship`: push the branch → open a PR → merge into `main` with a merge commit (never squash). |
+| [.claude/agents/doc-reviewer.md](.claude/agents/doc-reviewer.md) | Read-only agent that audits changed code against the commenting standard, accuracy first. |
+| [.claude/TODO.md](.claude/TODO.md) | Working task list, including the oversell-protection test plan. |
+| [.claude/settings.json](.claude/settings.json) | Hook configuration for the three scripts below. |

+| [scripts/branch_guard.py](scripts/branch_guard.py) | Keeps all work off `main`: flags a session that starts on `main`, blocks edits and commits there, and blocks direct pushes to `main` and squash merges. |
+| [scripts/check_kdoc.py](scripts/check_kdoc.py) | Reports missing KDoc after every edit to a `.kt` file. |
+| [scripts/export_sessions.py](scripts/export_sessions.py) | Exports session transcripts to `docs/ai-sessions/` after every Claude turn. |
+| [docs/ai-sessions/](docs/ai-sessions/) | Full transcripts of every session, including what I asked for and what I changed or rejected. |
+**Git workflow:** every piece of work happens on its own branch (`feature/…`, `fix/…`,
+`chore/…`) and reaches `main` only through a pull request merged by `/ship`, with the full
+commit history preserved.

content.content:
# Kotlin & Spring Concepts Index

A running index of every Kotlin and Spring concept used in this codebase. Each row
links to where the concept first appears. `/walkthrough` adds rows as new concepts
come up. For the full explanation, read the tagged comments in the code:

```sh
grep -rn "// Kotlin:" src    # language features
grep -rn "// Spring:" src    # framework behavior
grep -rn "// Why:" src       # design decisions
grep -rn "// Contract:" src  # lines that satisfy the OpenAPI contract
```

## Kotlin

| Concept | What it is | First seen |
| --- | --- | --- |

## Spring

| Concept | What it is | First seen |
| --- | --- | --- |
"""PostToolUse hook: flag non-private Kotlin declarations that have no KDoc.

Claude Code runs this after every Edit/Write (see .claude/settings.json) and pipes
the tool call as JSON on stdin. If the edited file is a .kt file and a class,
interface, object, typealias or function that is not private has no KDoc, the
script prints the gaps to stderr and exits 2. Claude Code then passes that output
back to Claude, which fixes it right away.

This is a line-based heuristic, not a Kotlin parser. It skips declarations inside
function bodies (local functions and classes) and `override` members, since those
inherit their docs. In src/test only classes are checked, because backtick test
names already describe themselves.

Can also be run by hand:  python scripts/check_kdoc.py path/to/File.kt
"""

from __future__ import annotations

import json
import re
import sys
from pathlib import Path

MODIFIERS = (
    r"(?:(?:public|internal|protected|open|abstract|final|data|sealed|enum|annotation|"
    r"inner|value|inline|suspend|operator|infix|tailrec|external|const|lateinit|expect|actual|"
    r"private|override)\s+)*"
)
DECL_RE = re.compile(
    r"^\s*" + MODIFIERS + r"(?:fun\s+interface|class|interface|object|fun|typealias)\b"
)
FUN_RE = re.compile(r"^\s*" + MODIFIERS + r"fun\b(?!\s+interface)")
TYPE_RE = re.compile(r"^\s*" + MODIFIERS + r"(?:fun\s+interface|class|interface|object|typealias)\b")
# Only the modifiers in front of the keyword count: `class Foo(private val x: Int)` is public.
SKIP_RE = re.compile(
    r"^\s*(?:\w+\s+)*?(?:private|override)\s+" + MODIFIERS
    + r"(?:fun\s+interface|class|interface|object|fun|typealias)\b"
)
STRING_RE = re.compile(r'"(?:\\.|[^"\\])*"')
ANNOTATION_RE = re.compile(r"^\s*@")
# `) = expr` or `): Type = expr` ends a signature with an expression body (no braces).
EXPR_BODY_RE = re.compile(r"\)\s*(?::[^={]*)?=(?!=)")


def strip_code(line: str) -> str:
    """Remove string literals and // comments so braces inside them are ignored."""
    line = STRING_RE.sub('""', line)
    return line.split("//", 1)[0]


def has_kdoc(lines: list[str], index: int) -> bool:
    """True if a KDoc block ends right above lines[index], allowing annotations in between."""
    i = index - 1
    while i >= 0 and (ANNOTATION_RE.match(lines[i]) or not lines[i].strip()):
        if not lines[i].strip():
            return False  # a blank line breaks the KDoc attachment
        i -= 1
    if i < 0 or not lines[i].rstrip().endswith("*/"):
        return False
    # Walk up to the start of the block and confirm it opens with /** (KDoc), not /*.

# Local Postgres for `./gradlew bootRun`.
#
# Spring: you never run `docker compose up` yourself. spring-boot-docker-compose (see
# build.gradle.kts) finds this file on startup, starts the container, waits until Postgres
# accepts connections, and configures the DataSource from the settings below. It stops the
# container again when the app shuts down. Tests don't use this file; they use Testcontainers.
services:
  postgres:
    # Why: pinned to a major version instead of `latest`, so a new Postgres release can't
    # change behavior underneath us. Keep in sync with support/TestcontainersConfiguration.kt.
    image: 'postgres:18'
    environment:
      # Local-only throwaway credentials; the container isn't reachable from outside this machine.
      - 'POSTGRES_DB=inventory'
      - 'POSTGRES_USER=inventory'
      - 'POSTGRES_PASSWORD=inventory'
    ports:
      # Why: only the container port is listed, so Docker picks a free host port. This avoids a
      # clash with any Postgres already running on 5432. Spring reads the mapped port from Docker.
      - '5432'

# /walkthrough the project scaffold on chore/project-scaffold: build.gradle.kts, settings.gradle.kts, compose.yaml, application.yml, InventoryApplication.kt, TestcontainersConfiguration.kt, InventoryApplicationTests.kt

Robert is learning Kotlin through this project. He has to understand the code well
enough to explain and defend it in an interview. Go at his pace. This is a
conversation, not a lecture.

## 1. Establish scope

- If `the project scaffold on chore/project-scaffold: build.gradle.kts, settings.gradle.kts, compose.yaml, application.yml, InventoryApplication.kt, TestcontainersConfiguration.kt, InventoryApplicationTests.kt` names files, a commit range or a topic, use that.
- Otherwise, find the last walkthrough log in `docs/learning/walkthroughs/` and read the
  commit SHA it records. The scope is `<that sha>..HEAD` plus any uncommitted changes.
  If there are no logs yet, the scope is everything under `src/` plus the build files.

Show the list of files in scope. Order them along the path a request takes:
build/config → entry point → controller → service → repository/model → error handling → tests.
Ask whether that order works for him before starting.

## 2. Walk through one file at a time

For each file:

1. **Role.** One or two sentences on what this file is for and how a request reaches it.
2. **Code in small chunks** (roughly 5–20 lines). Quote each chunk with its `path:line` reference, then explain:
   - every Kotlin feature in it: what it does, why it's idiomatic, and what the Java
     equivalent would look like when that comparison helps;
   - any Spring behavior that isn't visible in the code (what the framework does with the
     annotation, when the object is created, what runs before and after);
   - the design decision, and the alternative we rejected and why.
3. **Pause.** Ask whether he has questions about the file. Then ask one short
   check-your-understanding question, for example: "What happens if `quantity` is 0 here?"
   or "Why is this a `val`?" or "What would the response be if the SKU doesn't exist?"
   **Wait for his reply before moving to the next file.** Don't answer your own question.
4. If his answer is wrong or partial, re-explain it another way. Don't just repeat the
   explanation.
5. If a question shows that a code comment is unclear or wrong, offer to fix the comment.

Where a quick experiment would help, suggest one he can run himself, such as changing a
value and rerunning a test to watch it fail, or a `curl` call against the running app.

## 3. Wrap up

Yes, I think you're right. And I'd argue the current style hurts more than readability:

- **The reviewers will read this code.** At 3–4 lines of comments per line of code, the code looks like a tutorial rather than something you'd ship. Clean code with a separate study guide makes a better impression.
- **I broke our own rule.** CLAUDE.md already says longer explanations belong in `docs/learning/`. I put them inline anyway.

I'd take your idea with one change: keep the notes in `docs/learning/`, not literally next to each file. A `.md` file under `src/main/kotlin/` would sit in the source tree reviewers read, and one under `src/main/resources/` would get packaged into the jar.

## Proposal

**1. The code keeps only what a good production codebase would keep:**
- short KDoc on each declaration, which the hook still enforces;
- `// Why:` and `// Contract:` comments, one line each. These record decisions and are worth reviewers seeing.
- no `// Kotlin:` or `// Spring:` teaching comments in the code.

**2. A study-notes file per source file, mirroring the `src/` tree:**
```text
docs/learning/notes/
  build.gradle.kts.md
  compose.yaml.md
  main/InventoryApplication.kt.md
  test/support/TestcontainersConfiguration.kt.md
```
Each note walks its file top to bottom. It quotes each small chunk of code and explains it underneath, using the same `Kotlin:` / `Spring:` / `Why:` headings so it's still searchable. Quoting the code instead of citing line numbers means the notes don't go stale every time a line moves. This is also what `/walkthrough` would work from.

`InventoryApplication.kt` would shrink to this:

```kotlin
/**
 * Entry point of the inventory service. Component scanning starts from this package,
 * so every controller, service and repository below it is picked up automatically.
 */
@SpringBootApplication
class InventoryApplication

/** Starts Spring: builds the context, runs Flyway migrations, starts Tomcat. */
fun main(args: Array<String>) {
    runApplication<InventoryApplication>(*args)
}
```

**3. The tooling gets updated to match.** The CLAUDE.md commenting standard, the `doc-reviewer` agent, and the `/feature` and `/walkthrough` skills would all say that every `.kt` file needs a matching notes file. `doc-reviewer` would check the notes for accuracy.

**The trade-off:** a notes file can drift out of sync with its code. Quoting the code instead of citing line numbers helps. `doc-reviewer` will also flag any note that quotes code that no longer exists.

Separately, [InventoryApplication.kt](src/main/kotlin/com/robertwoolbright/inventory/InventoryApplication.kt) on disk is back to my first draft, with the `//` comments between the KDoc and the declarations. Was that you? It doesn't matter much, since this change rewrites the file anyway.

You review code in a Kotlin + Spring Boot project that doubles as a Kotlin learning
project for its author, Robert. The comments are part of how he learns. Check whether
someone new to Kotlin and Spring could understand every changed line from the code
and its comments alone.

## Scope

Unless the prompt names specific files, review what changed:
`git diff --name-only HEAD` plus untracked files (`git ls-files --others --exclude-standard`),
limited to `*.kt`, `*.kts`, `application*.yml` and `application*.properties`.

Read `CLAUDE.md` first; its "Commenting and documentation standard" section is the rubric.
Also read `src/main/resources/openapi/inventory.yaml` so you can check `// Contract:` comments against it.

## What to check

1. **KDoc coverage and quality.** Every non-private class, interface, object and function has
   KDoc that says what it does, why it exists, and where it sits in the request flow. Flag
   KDoc that only restates the name ("Gets inventory.").
2. **Kotlin concepts explained.** Every Kotlin feature a Java or Kotlin beginner might not
   recognise has a `// Kotlin:` comment the first time it appears in the file: data classes,
   nullable types and `?.`/`?:`/`!!`, `val` vs `var`, primary constructors with properties,
   default and named arguments, `when`, extension functions, scope functions
   (`let`/`apply`/`also`/`run`/`with`), `object`/`companion object`, sealed types,
   string templates, lambdas and trailing-lambda syntax, `it`, collection operators, `require`/`check`.
3. **Spring behavior explained.** Every annotation and every piece of implicit behavior has a
   `// Spring:` comment: stereotypes, constructor injection, request mapping, `@RequestBody`
   deserialization, validation, exception handlers, response status and content type,
   test slices (`@WebMvcTest`, `@SpringBootTest`), `MockMvc`.
4. **Decisions recorded.** Non-obvious choices (concurrency handling, error mapping, data store,
   status codes for edge cases) have a `// Why:` comment that names the rejected alternative.
5. **Contract traceability.** Code that implements a specific contract rule (status codes,
   `text/plain` errors, `minimum: 1`, create-or-add semantics, insufficient-stock rejection)
   has a `// Contract:` comment, and that comment matches the YAML.
6. **Accuracy.** Comments that are wrong or out of date are the worst outcome, because Robert
   will learn the wrong thing. Check each claim against the code. Mark any doubtful claim
   about Kotlin or Spring semantics as a finding.
7. **Noise.** Flag comments that only narrate trivial syntax and teach nothing.

## Output

Return a findings list grouped by file, each with `path:line`, the category (1–7 above),
what is missing or wrong, and a suggested comment. Put accuracy problems first. End
with a one-line verdict: `PASS` (no findings in categories 1–6) or `NEEDS WORK`.
Do not edit files. You are read-only.

    # Walk up to the start of the block and confirm it opens with /** (KDoc), not /*.
    while i >= 0 and "/*" not in lines[i]:
        i -= 1
    return i >= 0 and "/**" in lines[i]


def find_gaps(path: Path) -> list[str]:
    lines = path.read_text(encoding="utf-8").splitlines()
    is_test = "src/test" in path.as_posix()
    gaps: list[str] = []
    stack: list[str] = []  # one entry per open brace: "fun" or "block"
    pending_fun = False  # saw a fun signature whose body brace hasn't opened yet
    in_block_comment = False

    for n, raw in enumerate(lines):
        if in_block_comment:
            if "*/" in raw:
                in_block_comment = False
                raw = raw.split("*/", 1)[1]
            else:
                continue
        code = strip_code(raw)
        if "/*" in code:
            before, after = code.split("/*", 1)
            if "*/" not in after:
                in_block_comment = True
            code = before + (after.split("*/", 1)[1] if "*/" in after else "")

        inside_fun = "fun" in stack
        is_fun_decl = bool(FUN_RE.match(code))

        if not inside_fun and DECL_RE.match(code) and not SKIP_RE.match(code):
            if (not is_test or TYPE_RE.match(code)) and not has_kdoc(lines, n):
                gaps.append(f"{path}:{n + 1}: missing KDoc -> {raw.strip()}")

        if is_fun_decl and not inside_fun:
            pending_fun = True
        for ch in code:
            if ch == "{":
                stack.append("fun" if pending_fun or inside_fun else "block")
                pending_fun = False
            elif ch == "}" and stack:
                stack.pop()
        # Expression-bodied functions (`fun x() = ...`) never open a brace.
        if pending_fun and EXPR_BODY_RE.search(code):
            pending_fun = False

    return gaps


def main() -> int:
    if len(sys.argv) > 1:
        files = [Path(p) for p in sys.argv[1:]]
    else:
        try:
            payload = json.load(sys.stdin)
        except json.JSONDecodeError:
            return 0
        file_path = (payload.get("tool_input") or {}).get("file_path")
        if not file_path:
            return 0
        files = [Path(file_path)]

    gaps = [g for f in files if f.suffix == ".kt" and f.is_file() for g in find_gaps(f)]
    if not gaps:
        return 0
    print(
        "KDoc required on every non-private declaration (see CLAUDE.md, "
        "'Commenting and documentation standard'). Add KDoc for:\n" + "\n".join(gaps),
        file=sys.stderr,
    )
    return 2

def find_gaps(path: Path) -> list[str]:
    lines = path.read_text(encoding="utf-8").splitlines()
    is_test = "src/test" in path.as_posix()
    gaps: list[str] = []
    stack: list[str] = []  # one entry per open brace: "fun" or "block"
    pending_fun = False  # saw a fun signature whose body brace hasn't opened yet
    in_block_comment = False

    for n, raw in enumerate(lines):
        if in_block_comment:
            if "*/" in raw:
                in_block_comment = False
                raw = raw.split("*/", 1)[1]
            else:
                continue
        code = strip_code(raw)
        if "/*" in code:
            before, after = code.split("/*", 1)
            if "*/" not in after:
                in_block_comment = True
            code = before + (after.split("*/", 1)[1] if "*/" in after else "")

        inside_fun = "fun" in stack
        is_fun_decl = bool(FUN_RE.match(code))

        if not inside_fun and DECL_RE.match(code) and not SKIP_RE.match(code):
            if (not is_test or TYPE_RE.match(code)) and not has_kdoc(lines, n):
                gaps.append(f"{path}:{n + 1}: missing KDoc -> {raw.strip()}")

        if is_fun_decl and not inside_fun:
            pending_fun = True
        for ch in code:
            if ch == "{":
                stack.append("fun" if pending_fun or inside_fun else "block")
                pending_fun = False
            elif ch == "}" and stack:

# build.gradle.kts

> Source: [build.gradle.kts](../../../build.gradle.kts) · Last synced with code: 2026-09-23

## Role

The build definition: which compiler and plugins to use, which libraries the app and tests
depend on, and how tests run. Generated by Spring Initializr (the command is in the commit
"Generate the Spring Boot project with Spring Initializr") and then trimmed.

## Walkthrough

### The file is Kotlin: trailing lambdas

```kotlin
plugins {
    ...
}
```

**Kotlin:** `plugins { ... }` is a *function call*. Its only argument is a lambda, and Kotlin
lets a lambda that is the last argument move outside the parentheses. When it's the only
argument, the parentheses disappear entirely. So `plugins { }` is really `plugins({ })`.
Inside the lambda, `this` is a Gradle object (a "lambda with receiver"), which is why you can
call `id(...)` or `kotlin(...)` without a prefix. This pattern is called a **type-safe builder**,
and it's how Kotlin DSLs (Gradle, Ktor, kotlinx.html) read like configuration.

### Plugins

```kotlin
kotlin("jvm") version "2.3.21"
// Opens Spring-annotated classes: Kotlin classes are final by default, Spring needs to subclass some.
kotlin("plugin.spring") version "2.3.21"
id("org.springframework.boot") version "4.1.1"
// Supplies versions from Spring Boot's BOM, so most dependencies below have none.
id("io.spring.dependency-management") version "1.1.7"
```

**Kotlin:** `kotlin("jvm")` is shorthand for `id("org.jetbrains.kotlin.jvm")`. `version` is an
**infix function**: `a version b` means `a.version(b)`. Any single-argument function marked
`infix` can be called that way.

- **`kotlin("jvm")`**: runs the Kotlin compiler and targets the JVM.
- **`kotlin("plugin.spring")`**: Kotlin classes and functions are **final by default** (Java is
  the opposite; you have to write `final`). Spring sometimes creates a runtime *subclass* of
  your bean (a proxy) to add behavior, e.g. `@Transactional` or `@Configuration`, and it can't
  subclass a final class. This compiler plugin ("all-open") automatically makes classes with
  Spring annotations `open`, so we don't have to write `open` everywhere.
- **`org.springframework.boot`**: adds `bootRun` (run from source) and `bootJar` (one runnable
  "fat" jar that contains all dependencies).
- **`io.spring.dependency-management`**: imports Spring Boot's **BOM** (bill of materials), a
  list of library versions tested together.

**Why:** we have no version catalog (`libs.versions.toml`). The BOM already pins nearly every
version, so a catalog would add indirection for no benefit.

### Group, version and the Java toolchain

```kotlin
group = "com.robertwoolbright"
version = "0.0.1-SNAPSHOT"

java {
    toolchain {
        languageVersion = JavaLanguageVersion.of(21)
    }
}
```

**Kotlin:** `languageVersion = ...` looks like a field assignment. Gradle properties are lazy
`Property<T>` objects, though, and Gradle's Kotlin DSL turns `=` into a call to `.set(...)`.
Older builds write `languageVersion.set(JavaLanguageVersion.of(21))`.

**Why:** a toolchain makes Gradle compile and test with JDK 21, whichever JDK is running Gradle
itself (Gradle finds or downloads one). Anyone who clones the repo builds with the same Java
version. The Kotlin plugin reads the toolchain too, so the bytecode targets Java 21.

### Dependencies: configurations

```kotlin
dependencies {
    implementation("org.springframework.boot:spring-boot-starter-flyway")
    ...
    developmentOnly("org.springframework.boot:spring-boot-docker-compose")
    runtimeOnly("org.postgresql:postgresql")
    testImplementation(...)
    testRuntimeOnly("org.junit.platform:junit-platform-launcher")
}
```

The function name in front of each dependency (its *configuration*) decides where it's visible:

| Configuration | Visible to |
| --- | --- |
| `implementation` | app code at compile time and at runtime |
| `runtimeOnly` | runtime only; our code never refers to it by name |
| `developmentOnly` | `bootRun` only; left out of tests and of the jar |
| `testImplementation` / `testRuntimeOnly` | the same idea, for `src/test` |

**Spring:** a **starter** is a dependency that brings a coherent set of libraries plus the
auto-configuration for them. Spring Boot 4 split the starters into smaller modules, which is why
Flyway, JDBC and Web MVC each have their own starter and test starter.

### App dependencies

| Dependency | What it gives us |
| --- | --- |
| `spring-boot-starter-flyway` | Runs the SQL migrations in `src/main/resources/db/migration` at startup, before any request is served. |
| `flyway-database-postgresql` | Since Flyway 10, support for each database is a separate module. Without it, Flyway refuses to talk to Postgres. |
| `spring-boot-starter-jdbc` | A pooled `DataSource` (HikariCP), `JdbcClient`/`JdbcTemplate` and a transaction manager, all auto-configured. `JdbcClient` is our data-access API. |
| `spring-boot-starter-webmvc` | Spring MVC on an embedded Tomcat, plus Jackson for JSON. (Boot 4 renamed `starter-web` to `starter-webmvc`.) |
| `kotlin-reflect` | Lets Spring read Kotlin metadata that Java reflection can't see, such as whether a parameter is nullable and whether it has a default value. |
| `jackson-module-kotlin` | Teaches Jackson to build Kotlin classes. A `data class` has no no-arg constructor and no setters; this module calls the primary constructor and respects non-null types and default values. `tools.jackson` is **Jackson 3**'s group ID (Boot 4 moved to Jackson 3). |
| `spring-boot-docker-compose` | On `bootRun`, runs `docker compose up` on `compose.yaml` and points the DataSource at it. See [compose.yaml notes](compose.yaml.md). |
| `postgresql` | The JDBC driver. We code only against the standard `java.sql` interfaces, so it's `runtimeOnly`. |

### Test dependencies

| Dependency | What it gives us |
| --- | --- |
| `spring-boot-starter-{flyway,jdbc,webmvc}-test` | Test support for each module, e.g. `@WebMvcTest` + `MockMvc` and `@JdbcTest`. They also pull in `spring-boot-starter-test`: JUnit 5, AssertJ, Mockito. |
| `spring-boot-testcontainers` | `@ServiceConnection`, which turns a running container into DataSource settings. |
| `kotlin-test-junit5` | `kotlin.test` assertions (`assertEquals`, `assertFailsWith`) backed by JUnit 5. |
| `testcontainers-junit-jupiter`, `testcontainers-postgresql` | Start a real Postgres in Docker for tests. |
| `junit-platform-launcher` | Gradle 9 no longer bundles the JUnit Platform launcher; it has to be on the test runtime classpath. |

**Why:** tests run against real Postgres instead of H2, an in-memory database that imitates
others. Our oversell protection depends on Postgres-specific behavior (`ON CONFLICT`, row locks
during `UPDATE`, `CHECK` constraints), and H2 imitates those imperfectly.

### Compiler options

```kotlin
kotlin {
    compilerOptions {
        freeCompilerArgs.addAll("-Xjsr305=strict", "-Xannotation-default-target=param-property")
    }
}
```

**Kotlin:** Kotlin's null safety (`String` can never be null; `String?` can) stops at the edge of
Java code, because Java types carry no nullability. Kotlin treats an unannotated Java type as a
**platform type**, shown as `String!`: you may treat it as nullable or not, and if you guess
wrong you get a runtime NPE. Many Java libraries annotate their APIs instead.
- **`-Xjsr305=strict`**: turns the JSR-305 annotations (`@Nonnull` / `@Nullable`) into real
  `String` / `String?` types, so a mistake becomes a compile error. Spring Framework 7 uses the
  newer JSpecify annotations, which Kotlin 2 already enforces; this flag covers libraries still
  on JSR-305.
- **`-Xannotation-default-target=param-property`**: in `class Q(@Ann val x: Int)`, the one
  `val x` is a constructor parameter, a property and a backing field all at once, so an
  annotation on it is ambiguous. This option puts it on the parameter **and** on the property (or
  on the field if there's no property). That's where Jackson and Bean Validation look for
  annotations. It will become Kotlin's default in a future release.

### Tests use JUnit 5

```kotlin
tasks.withType<Test> {
    useJUnitPlatform()
}
```

**Kotlin:** `withType<Test>` uses a **reified type parameter**. On the JVM, generic types are
normally erased at runtime, but an `inline` function can mark its type parameter `reified` and
use it as a real class. So you write `withType<Test>` instead of Java's
`withType(Test.class)`. The trailing lambda then configures every `Test` task.

## Check your understanding

- Why does `postgresql` use `runtimeOnly` and not `implementation`? What would break if it were `compileOnly`?
- Remove `kotlin("plugin.spring")`. Which kind of class would Spring fail on, and why?
- What does `-Xjsr305=strict` change about a Java method annotated `@Nullable String find()` when called from Kotlin?

## Role

The build definition: which compiler and plugins to use, which libraries the app and tests
depend on, and how tests run. Generated by Spring Initializr (the command is in the commit
"Generate the Spring Boot project with Spring Initializr") and then trimmed.

## Walkthrough

### The file is Kotlin: trailing lambdas

```kotlin
plugins {
    ...
}
```

**Kotlin:** `plugins { ... }` is a *function call*. Its only argument is a lambda, and Kotlin
lets a lambda that is the last argument move outside the parentheses. When it's the only
argument, the parentheses disappear entirely. So `plugins { }` is really `plugins({ })`.
Inside the lambda, `this` is a Gradle object (a "lambda with receiver"), which is why you can
call `id(...)` or `kotlin(...)` without a prefix. This pattern is called a **type-safe builder**,
and it's how Kotlin DSLs (Gradle, Ktor, kotlinx.html) read like configuration.

### Plugins

```kotlin
kotlin("jvm") version "2.3.21"
// Opens Spring-annotated classes: Kotlin classes are final by default, Spring needs to subclass some.
kotlin("plugin.spring") version "2.3.21"
id("org.springframework.boot") version "4.1.1"
// Supplies versions from Spring Boot's BOM, so most dependencies below have none.
id("io.spring.dependency-management") version "1.1.7"
```

**Kotlin:** `kotlin("jvm")` is shorthand for `id("org.jetbrains.kotlin.jvm")`. `version` is an
**infix function**: `a version b` means `a.version(b)`. Any single-argument function marked
`infix` can be called that way.

  the opposite; you have to write `final`). Spring sometimes creates a runtime *subclass* of
  your bean (a proxy) to add behavior, e.g. `@Transactional` or `@Configuration`, and it can't
  subclass a final class. This compiler plugin ("all-open") automatically makes classes with
  Spring annotations `open`, so we don't have to write `open` everywhere.

  "fat" jar that contains all dependencies).
- **`io.spring.dependency-management`**: imports Spring Boot's **BOM** (bill of materials), a
  list of library versions tested together.

**Why:** we have no version catalog (`libs.versions.toml`). The BOM already pins nearly every
version, so a catalog would add indirection for no benefit.

```kotlin
group = "com.robertwoolbright"
version = "0.0.1-SNAPSHOT"

java {
    toolchain {
        languageVersion = JavaLanguageVersion.of(21)
    }
}
```

`Property<T>` objects, though, and Gradle's Kotlin DSL turns `=` into a call to `.set(...)`.
Older builds write `languageVersion.set(JavaLanguageVersion.of(21))`.

itself (Gradle finds or downloads one). Anyone who clones the repo builds with the same Java

```kotlin
    ...
    developmentOnly("org.springframework.boot:spring-boot-docker-compose")
    runtimeOnly("org.postgresql:postgresql")
    testImplementation(...)
    testRuntimeOnly("org.junit.platform:junit-platform-launcher")
}
```

The function name in front of each dependency (its *configuration*) decides where it's visible:

| Configuration | Visible to |
| --- | --- |
| `implementation` | app code at compile time and at runtime |
| `runtimeOnly` | runtime only; our code never refers to it by name |

| Dependency | What it gives us |
| --- | --- |
| `spring-boot-starter-flyway` | Runs the SQL migrations in `src/main/resources/db/migration` at startup, before any request is served. |
| `flyway-database-postgresql` | Since Flyway 10, support for each database is a separate module. Without it, Flyway refuses to talk to Postgres. |
| `spring-boot-starter-jdbc` | A pooled `DataSource` (HikariCP), `JdbcClient`/`JdbcTemplate` and a transaction manager, all auto-configured. `JdbcClient` is our data-access API. |

# compose.yaml

> Source: [compose.yaml](../../../compose.yaml) · Last synced with code: 2026-09-23

## Role

Defines the Postgres container used when you run the app locally with `./gradlew bootRun`.
Tests don't use it; they use Testcontainers (see
[TestcontainersConfiguration notes](test/support/TestcontainersConfiguration.kt.md)).

## Walkthrough

### Who runs this file

```yaml
# Local Postgres for `./gradlew bootRun`. Spring Boot's Docker Compose support starts and stops
# it automatically. Tests don't use this file; they use Testcontainers.
```

**Spring:** you never run `docker compose up` yourself. The `spring-boot-docker-compose`
dependency (`developmentOnly` in the build) finds `compose.yaml` at startup, starts it, and waits
until Postgres reports healthy. It then reads the container's image, environment and mapped port
and builds the DataSource connection details from them (a JDBC URL, user and password). On
shutdown it stops the container. You can see this in the `bootRun` log: `Container ... Started`,
then `Healthy`, then Flyway connecting to `jdbc:postgresql://127.0.0.1:<port>/inventory`.

### Image version

```yaml
image: 'postgres:18'
```

**Why:** pinned to a major version instead of `latest`, so a new Postgres major release can't
change behavior without us noticing. `18` still receives patch releases (18.6, 18.7, …). Tests
use the same tag, so local runs and tests behave the same.

### Credentials

```yaml
environment:
  - 'POSTGRES_DB=inventory'
  - 'POSTGRES_USER=inventory'
  - 'POSTGRES_PASSWORD=inventory'
```

The official Postgres image creates this database and user on first start. These are throwaway,
local-only values. Spring reads them from here, so they aren't repeated in `application.yml`.

### Ports

```yaml
ports:
  - '5432'
```

**Why:** only the *container* port is listed, so Docker maps it to a random free host port (e.g.
`127.0.0.1:53106`). `'5432:5432'` would fail if you already had Postgres running locally.
Spring asks Docker which port it got, so nothing needs to know the number in advance.

## Check your understanding

- If you run `docker compose up` yourself and then `bootRun`, what do you expect Spring to do?
- Why doesn't `application.yml` need a `spring.datasource.url`?

# application.yml

> Source: [src/main/resources/application.yml](../../../../../src/main/resources/application.yml) · Last synced with code: 2026-09-23

## Role

Spring Boot's configuration file. Spring loads it from the classpath at startup, and anything it
doesn't set keeps its auto-configured default.

## Walkthrough

### What isn't here

```yaml
# Why: no spring.datasource.* here. Docker Compose support (bootRun) and Testcontainers'
# @ServiceConnection (tests) supply the connection details, so no credentials live in config.
```

**Spring:** auto-configuration builds a `DataSource` from *connection details*. Usually those come
from `spring.datasource.url`, `username` and `password`. Docker Compose support and
`@ServiceConnection` both register a `JdbcConnectionDetails` bean that takes priority over those
properties, so the database is wherever the container is.

**Why:** this means no hard-coded port and no password in a committed file. In production you'd
set `SPRING_DATASOURCE_URL` and friends as environment variables; Spring maps environment
variables onto these properties automatically ("relaxed binding").

### The application name

```yaml
spring:
  application:
    name: inventory
```

It appears in every log line (`--- [inventory]`) and identifies the service to tools such as
metrics and tracing.

**Why YAML instead of `.properties`:** they're equivalent (`spring.application.name=inventory`).
YAML groups nested keys, which reads better once there are several `spring.*` settings.

# InventoryApplication.kt

> Source: [src/main/kotlin/com/robertwoolbright/inventory/InventoryApplication.kt](../../../../src/main/kotlin/com/robertwoolbright/inventory/InventoryApplication.kt) · Last synced with code: 2026-09-23

## Role

The entry point. `./gradlew bootRun` (or `java -jar`) calls `main`, which starts Spring. Spring
then finds every controller, service and repository and wires them together. No request ever
passes through this file, but none could be served without it.

## Walkthrough

### The package

```kotlin
package com.robertwoolbright.inventory
```

**Kotlin:** same as Java, except the directory doesn't *have* to match the package in Kotlin. We
keep them matching anyway because that's the convention and Spring's scan relies on packages.

**Why:** this file sits in the *root* package on purpose. See `@ComponentScan` below.

### `@SpringBootApplication` and a class with no body

```kotlin
@SpringBootApplication
class InventoryApplication
```

**Spring:** `@SpringBootApplication` combines three annotations:

| Annotation | Effect |
| --- | --- |
| `@Configuration` | This class may declare `@Bean` methods. |
| `@EnableAutoConfiguration` | Configure whatever the classpath implies: Tomcat because Web MVC is present, a `DataSource` because JDBC + the Postgres driver are, Flyway, Jackson… |
| `@ComponentScan` | Find `@Component`, `@Service`, `@Repository` and `@RestController` classes **in this package and its sub-packages**, and create them as beans. |

That scan is why the file lives at `com.robertwoolbright.inventory`: the future
`inventory.InventoryController` sits below it and gets found automatically.

**Kotlin:** a class with no body needs no `{}`. Spring never calls anything on this class; it
only reads the annotations. It must still be a `class` rather than an `object` (Kotlin's
singleton), because Spring wants to create and proxy configuration classes itself. The
`plugin.spring` compiler plugin makes it `open` so Spring can subclass it. See the
[build notes](../build.gradle.kts.md).

### Top-level `main`

```kotlin
/** Starts Spring: builds the application context, runs Flyway migrations and starts Tomcat. */
fun main(args: Array<String>) {
    runApplication<InventoryApplication>(*args)
}
```

**Kotlin: top-level functions.** `main` isn't inside any class. Kotlin allows functions at file
level. The compiler still has to put bytecode in a class, so it generates one named after the
file: `InventoryApplicationKt`, with a `public static void main(String[] args)`. The startup log
shows it: `Started InventoryApplicationKt in 5.9 seconds`. In Java, `main` must be a static
method written inside a class.

**Kotlin: `Array<String>`** is Java's `String[]`. Kotlin arrays are an ordinary generic class, not
special syntax.

**Kotlin: reified generics.** `runApplication<InventoryApplication>(...)` names the class in angle
brackets. It's an `inline` function with a `reified` type parameter, so it can use `T::class` at
runtime (normally generics are erased). The Java equivalent:
`SpringApplication.run(InventoryApplication.class, args)`.

**Kotlin: spread operator.** `runApplication` takes `vararg args: String`. Passing `args` alone
would pass *one* argument, the array itself. `*args` spreads the array's elements into the
vararg. (Java converts between arrays and varargs automatically; Kotlin makes you say so.)

**Spring:** `runApplication` creates the application context. It runs auto-configuration,
creates every bean (including the Flyway bean, which applies migrations while starting up),
starts Tomcat on port 8080, and then returns. The JVM stays alive because Tomcat's threads
are still running.

## Check your understanding

- If `InventoryController` were put in package `com.robertwoolbright.web`, would Spring find it? Why?
- What is the name of the JVM class that contains `main`, and why?
- What would `runApplication<InventoryApplication>(args)` (no `*`) pass to Spring?

> Source: [src/test/kotlin/com/robertwoolbright/inventory/support/TestcontainersConfiguration.kt](../../../../../src/test/kotlin/com/robertwoolbright/inventory/support/TestcontainersConfiguration.kt) · Last synced with code: 2026-09-23

## Role

Shared test setup. Any test that imports it gets a real Postgres 18 running in Docker, with the
app's DataSource pointed at it. Every repository, controller and concurrency test builds on this.

## Walkthrough

### `@TestConfiguration(proxyBeanMethods = false)`

```kotlin
@TestConfiguration(proxyBeanMethods = false)
class TestcontainersConfiguration {
```

**Spring:** `@TestConfiguration` is a `@Configuration` meant only for tests. Component scanning
from `@SpringBootApplication` deliberately skips it, so the container exists only in tests that
ask for it with `@Import(TestcontainersConfiguration::class)`.

**Spring: `proxyBeanMethods`.** By default Spring subclasses a `@Configuration` class so that
when one `@Bean` method calls another, you get the existing bean instead of a new object. We have
one bean and no such calls, so turning the proxy off is faster and changes nothing.

**Kotlin: named arguments.** `proxyBeanMethods = false` names the parameter it sets. Kotlin
allows named arguments in any function call, and annotations use the same syntax. Named
arguments are most useful for boolean flags, since `TestConfiguration(false)` would say nothing.

### The container bean

```kotlin
@Bean
@ServiceConnection
fun postgresContainer(): PostgreSQLContainer =
    // Why: same major version as compose.yaml, so tests and local runs behave the same.
    PostgreSQLContainer(DockerImageName.parse("postgres:18"))
```

**Spring: `@Bean`.** The return value becomes a Spring-managed object. Testcontainers containers
are `Startable`, and Spring Boot starts them when the bean is created and stops them when the
context closes.

**Spring: `@ServiceConnection`.** This annotation is what connects the container to the app. Spring Boot sees a
`PostgreSQLContainer`, asks it for its JDBC URL, username and password (random host port, test
credentials), and registers them as the connection details. Those override any
`spring.datasource.*` setting.

**Spring: context caching.** Spring caches test application contexts and reuses them between test
classes with identical configuration. Every test class that imports this configuration shares
one context, and therefore one container, instead of starting a fresh Postgres each time.

**Kotlin: expression body.** `fun f(): T = expr` replaces `fun f(): T { return expr }` when the
body is a single expression. The return type could be inferred, but we keep it because it's
part of what this function promises.

**Why:** a real Postgres rather than H2. See the [build notes](../../build.gradle.kts.md).

## Check your understanding

- What starts the container: JUnit, Testcontainers, or Spring? When does it stop?
- If two test classes both import this configuration, how many Postgres containers run?

# InventoryApplicationTests.kt

> Source: [src/test/kotlin/com/robertwoolbright/inventory/InventoryApplicationTests.kt](../../../../src/test/kotlin/com/robertwoolbright/inventory/InventoryApplicationTests.kt) · Last synced with code: 2026-09-23

## Role

A smoke test that checks the whole application can start. It's the cheapest test that
catches a broken dependency, a bad config file or a failing migration.

## Walkthrough

### Starting the real application in a test

```kotlin
@Import(TestcontainersConfiguration::class)
@SpringBootTest
class InventoryApplicationTests {
```

**Spring: `@SpringBootTest`.** Finds `@SpringBootApplication` by searching up the package tree, then
starts the *full* application context, the same one `main` builds. (Test "slices" such as
`@WebMvcTest` start only part of it; we'll use those for controller tests.) Here there's no web
server, because `@SpringBootTest` uses a mock web environment unless told otherwise.

**Spring: `@Import`.** Adds the Postgres container from `support/` to this context. Without it
there's no database, the DataSource can't be configured, and the context fails to start.

**Kotlin: class references.** `TestcontainersConfiguration::class` is a `KClass`, Kotlin's
equivalent of Java's `TestcontainersConfiguration.class`. For an annotation argument Kotlin passes
the Java class automatically.

### An empty test that still tests something

```kotlin
/** Passes as long as the Spring context starts; the empty body is intentional. */
@Test
fun contextLoads() {
}
```

The work happens before the method runs. JUnit asks Spring's test extension to prepare the test
instance, which starts the context. If that fails, the test fails. So "passes" means every bean
was created, Postgres was reachable and Flyway applied every migration.

**Kotlin:** JUnit 5 doesn't need test classes or methods to be `public` or `open`. Kotlin's
defaults (public, final) are fine.

## Check your understanding

- Delete the `@Import` line and run `./gradlew test`. What error do you predict, and at which step does it happen?
- Why is `contextLoads` worth keeping once there are more detailed tests?

"""Stop hook: every source file must have study notes that are at least as new as the code.

The code carries only short KDoc and one-line `// Why:` / `// Contract:` comments. The teaching
lives in docs/learning/notes/, one Markdown file per source file (see the README there for the
mapping). This hook keeps the two from drifting apart.

Claude Code runs it when Claude is about to end its turn (see .claude/settings.json). For each
source file it compares "when did this last change" for the file and for its notes:

  - a file with uncommitted changes (modified, staged or untracked): its modification time
  - a committed, unchanged file: the time of the last commit that touched it

If the code is newer than its notes, or the notes are missing, the script prints what's stale to
stderr and exits 2. Claude Code then keeps Claude working with that message as feedback, and
Claude runs /sync-docs. It also reports notes whose source file no longer exists.

To avoid an endless loop, it never blocks twice in a row: when Claude Code says a Stop hook
already sent Claude back to work (`stop_hook_active`), the script lets the turn end.

Can also be run by hand, for example as a pre-ship check:  python scripts/check_notes.py
(exit 1 when something is stale).
"""

from __future__ import annotations

import json
import subprocess
import sys
from pathlib import Path

ROOT = Path(__file__).resolve().parent.parent
NOTES = Path("docs/learning/notes")
PACKAGE = "com/robertwoolbright/inventory/"

# (source prefix, notes prefix, which files under the prefix count as source)
MAPPINGS = [
    (f"src/main/kotlin/{PACKAGE}", "main/", lambda p: p.endswith(".kt")),
    (f"src/test/kotlin/{PACKAGE}", "test/", lambda p: p.endswith(".kt")),
    ("src/main/resources/", "main/resources/",
     lambda p: (p.count("/") == 0 and p.startswith("application") and p.endswith((".yml", ".yaml")))
     or (p.startswith("db/migration/") and p.endswith(".sql"))),
    ("", "", lambda p: "/" not in p and (p.endswith(".gradle.kts") or p == "compose.yaml")),
]


def git(*args: str) -> str:
    return subprocess.run(
        ["git", *args], cwd=ROOT, capture_output=True, text=True, encoding="utf-8", check=False
    ).stdout


def notes_path(source: str) -> str | None:
    """Map a repo-relative source path to its notes path, or None if it needs no notes."""
    for src_prefix, notes_prefix, is_source in MAPPINGS:
        if source.startswith(src_prefix):
            rest = source[len(src_prefix):]
            if is_source(rest):
                return (NOTES / f"{notes_prefix}{rest}.md").as_posix()
            return None
    return None


def dirty_paths() -> set[str]:
    """Repo-relative paths with uncommitted changes, including untracked files."""
    paths = set()
    for line in git("status", "--porcelain", "-uall").splitlines():
        path = line[3:]
        if " -> " in path:  # rename: "old -> new"
            path = path.split(" -> ", 1)[1]
        paths.add(path.strip('"'))
    return paths


def last_change(path: str, dirty: set[str]) -> float | None:
    """Seconds since the epoch when `path` last changed, or None if it doesn't exist."""
    full = ROOT / path
    if not full.is_file():
        return None
    if path in dirty:
        return full.stat().st_mtime
    committed = git("log", "-1", "--format=%ct", "--", path).strip()
    return float(committed) if committed else full.stat().st_mtime


def find_problems() -> list[str]:
    dirty = dirty_paths()
    tracked = set(git("ls-files").splitlines())
    sources = sorted(p for p in tracked | dirty if notes_path(p) and (ROOT / p).is_file())

    problems = []
    expected_notes = set()
    for source in sources:
        notes = notes_path(source)
        expected_notes.add(notes)
        source_time = last_change(source, dirty)
        notes_time = last_change(notes, dirty)
        if notes_time is None:
            problems.append(f"missing notes: {source} -> create {notes}")
        elif source_time is not None and source_time > notes_time:
            problems.append(f"stale notes:   {source} changed after {notes}")

    notes_dir = ROOT / NOTES
    if notes_dir.is_dir():
        for md in sorted(notes_dir.rglob("*.md")):
            rel = md.relative_to(ROOT).as_posix()
            if md.name != "README.md" and rel not in expected_notes:
                problems.append(f"orphan notes:  {rel} (its source file is gone; delete or move it)")
    return problems


def main() -> int:
    hook_mode = not sys.stdin.isatty()
    if hook_mode:
        try:
            payload = json.load(sys.stdin)
        except json.JSONDecodeError:
            payload = {}
        if payload.get("stop_hook_active"):
            return 0

    problems = find_problems()
    if not problems:
        return 0
    print(
        "Study notes are out of date (see docs/learning/notes/README.md). Run /sync-docs to update "
        "them. If a change really needs no new explanation, bump the notes' 'Last synced' date.\n"
        + "\n".join(problems),
        file=sys.stderr,
    )
    return 2 if hook_mode else 1


if __name__ == "__main__":
    sys.exit(main())

        source_time = last_change(source, dirty)
        notes_time = last_change(notes, dirty)
        if notes_time is None:
            problems.append(f"missing notes: {source} -> create {notes}")
        elif source_time is not None and source_time > notes_time:
            problems.append(f"stale notes:   {source} changed after {notes}")

    notes_dir = ROOT / NOTES
    if notes_dir.is_dir():
        for md in sorted(notes_dir.rglob("*.md")):
            rel = md.relative_to(ROOT).as_posix()
            if md.name != "README.md" and rel not in expected_notes:

    if hook_mode:
        try:
            payload = json.load(sys.stdin)

        if payload.get("stop_hook_active"):

    if not problems:

    print(

        "them. If a change really needs no new explanation, bump the notes' 'Last synced' date.\n"
        + "\n".join(problems),

    )
    return 2 if hook_mode else 1

    sys.exit(main())

name: sync-docs
description: Bring the project documentation in line with the code, covering the per-file study notes in docs/learning/notes/, the concepts index, the README and the TODO. Use after any code change, when the check_notes Stop hook reports stale or missing notes, and as a step of /feature.
argument-hint: "[files to sync; default: everything changed on this branch]"
---

# /sync-docs $ARGUMENTS

The code stays clean. The teaching lives in `docs/learning/notes/`, one notes file per source
file. This skill keeps every piece of documentation truthful after a code change. **Wrong
documentation is worse than missing documentation**, because Robert will learn from it.

## 1. Find what changed

If `$ARGUMENTS` names files, use those. Otherwise:

```sh
python scripts/check_notes.py            # stale / missing / orphan notes
git diff --name-only main...HEAD         # committed on this branch
git status --porcelain -uall             # uncommitted
```

Use `docs/learning/notes/README.md` to map each source file to its notes path.

## 2. Update each notes file

For each changed source file, read the **whole** source file, then its notes file, and edit
the notes to match. Follow the format in `docs/learning/notes/README.md`:

- **Role** section: where the file sits in controller → service → repository, and why it exists.
- **Walkthrough**: one `###` section per small chunk (about 5–20 lines), in file order. Quote the
  chunk *exactly as it is in the source* (no line numbers), then explain it under the
  `**Kotlin:**`, `**Spring:**`, `**Why:**` and `**Contract:**` labels:
  - every Kotlin feature a Java developer or Kotlin beginner wouldn't recognize, with the
    Java equivalent where it helps;
  - Spring behavior the code doesn't show (what an annotation causes, when objects are
    created, what runs before and after);
  - each design decision and the alternative we rejected;
  - for contract rules, the exact part of `src/main/resources/openapi/inventory.yaml` it satisfies.
- Explain a concept in full in the first notes file where it appears; elsewhere, link to that
  file instead of repeating it.
- **Check your understanding**: 1–3 questions that make Robert predict behavior. Don't include answers.
- Remove sections for code that no longer exists, and re-quote chunks that changed.
- Set `Last synced with code:` to today's date.
- A new source file gets a new notes file; a deleted one gets its notes deleted. A moved file
  gets its notes moved.

If a change truly needs no new explanation (for example a rename), still check that every quote
in the notes matches the code, then bump the date.

## 3. Keep the code comments slim

While reading the source, check it meets the in-code standard in `CLAUDE.md`: short KDoc on every
non-private declaration, one-line `// Why:` and `// Contract:` comments, and no teaching
`// Kotlin:` or `// Spring:` comments. Move any long explanation you find into the notes.

## 4. Update the indexes and project docs

- `docs/learning/kotlin-concepts.md`: add a row for each concept appearing for the first time,
  linking to the notes file that explains it. No duplicate rows.
- `README.md`: update anything the change affected: the endpoint status table, build/run
  commands, project layout, tech stack and versions, open decisions and decision records.
- `.claude/TODO.md`: check off finished items (with the date) and add any new ones.

## 5. Verify

1. Run `python scripts/check_notes.py`. It must print nothing and exit 0.
2. Launch the `doc-reviewer` agent on the changed files. Fix every accuracy finding, and rerun
   it until it returns `PASS`.
3. Tell Robert in a few lines which docs changed and what the reviewer caught.

---
name: doc-reviewer
description: Read-only reviewer that checks changed Kotlin, Gradle, Spring config and SQL files and their study notes (docs/learning/notes/) against this project's documentation standard in CLAUDE.md. Accuracy comes first. Use after /sync-docs, after implementing a feature, and before a walkthrough.
tools: Read, Grep, Glob, Bash
---

You review a Kotlin + Spring Boot project that doubles as a Kotlin learning project for its
author, Robert. The code is kept clean. The teaching lives in per-file study notes under
`docs/learning/notes/`. Your job is to check whether someone new to Kotlin and Spring could
understand every changed line from the code plus its notes, and whether everything the notes
say is **true**.

## Scope

Unless the prompt names specific files, review what changed on this branch:
`git diff --name-only main...HEAD` plus `git status --porcelain -uall`, limited to `*.kt`,
`*.kts`, `compose.yaml`, `application*.yml` and `db/migration/*.sql`, together with their notes
files. `docs/learning/notes/README.md` gives the mapping from source file to notes file.

Read `CLAUDE.md` first; its "Documentation standard" section is the rubric. Also read
`src/main/resources/openapi/inventory.yaml` so you can check `Contract` claims against it.
Run `python scripts/check_notes.py` and include anything it reports.

## What to check

1. **Accuracy.** This matters most. Check every claim in the notes and code comments against the
   code and against how Kotlin, Spring Boot 4 and Postgres actually behave. Mark any doubtful claim
   as a finding and say what you'd verify. Wrong notes teach Robert the wrong thing.
2. **Quotes match the code.** Every code block quoted in a notes file must appear in the
   source file (ignoring leading and trailing whitespace). A stale quote means the notes
   describe code that no longer exists.
3. **Coverage.** Every chunk of the source file is walked through in the notes, in file order.
   Every Kotlin feature a beginner might not recognize is explained where it first appears:
   data classes, nullable types and `?.`/`?:`/`!!`, `val` vs `var`, constructor properties,
   default and named arguments, `when`, extension functions, scope functions, `object`/companion,
   sealed types, string templates, lambdas and `it`, collection operators, `require`/`check`.
   So is every piece of Spring behavior the code doesn't show: stereotypes, constructor
   injection, request mapping, body deserialization, validation, exception handlers, status and
   content type, and test slices.
4. **Decisions and contract.** Non-obvious choices have a `Why` that names the rejected
   alternative. Contract rules (status codes, `text/plain` errors, `minimum: 1`, create-or-add,
   insufficient-stock rejection) have a `Contract` note or `// Contract:` comment that matches
   the YAML.
5. **The code stays slim.** KDoc on every non-private declaration, short and meaningful (not a
   restated name). Inline comments only for `// Why:` and `// Contract:`, one or two lines each.
   Flag teaching comments (`// Kotlin:`, `// Spring:`) or long explanations in code; they belong
   in the notes.
6. **Structure.** Notes follow the README format: source link, `Last synced` date, Role,
   Walkthrough, and Check your understanding (questions without answers). New concepts
   have a row in `docs/learning/kotlin-concepts.md`.

## Output

Return findings grouped by file (source or notes), each with `path:line`, the category (1–6),
what is wrong or missing, and a suggested fix. Put accuracy problems first. End with a
one-line verdict: `PASS` (no findings in categories 1–4) or `NEEDS WORK`. Do not edit files.
You are read-only.

## Commenting and documentation standard (teaching mode)

This goes further than normal production code on purpose. Follow it for every `.kt` file.

1. **KDoc on every non-private declaration**: classes, interfaces, objects, and functions.

   they can be searched (`grep -rn "// Kotlin:" src`):

     scope functions, extension functions, `when`, default arguments, sealed types...).

     does, how dependency injection wires this, what auto-configuration provides,
     how a request is mapped or a response is serialized.
   - `// Why:` a design decision and the alternative that was rejected.
   - `// Contract:` the line exists to satisfy a specific part of inventory.yaml.
3. Explain a concept in full the first time it appears in a file. After that, a short
   tag is enough. Longer explanations go in [docs/learning/kotlin-concepts.md](docs/learning/kotlin-concepts.md).
4. Do not narrate trivial statements (`// increment counter`). Every comment should
   teach something or record a decision.
5. `build.gradle.kts` and `application.yml` get the same treatment: comment each plugin,
   dependency and setting with what it is for.

# CLAUDE.md

Project memory for Claude Code. Loaded automatically at the start of every session.

## What this project is

A take-home assessment for Nuuly: a small inventory REST API (receive stock by SKU,
process purchases, report inventory levels). Full brief: [docs/Nuuly_Assessment_Instructions.txt](docs/Nuuly_Assessment_Instructions.txt).

**It is also a Kotlin master class.** Robert is learning Kotlin and wants to use this
project to learn it properly, whatever happens with the interview. Every piece of
code must teach as well as work. Treat "can Robert explain every line of this in the

# CLAUDE.md

Project memory for Claude Code. Loaded automatically at the start of every session.

## What this project is

A take-home assessment for Nuuly: a small inventory REST API (receive stock by SKU,
process purchases, report inventory levels). Full brief: [docs/Nuuly_Assessment_Instructions.txt](docs/Nuuly_Assessment_Instructions.txt).

**It is also a Kotlin master class.** Robert is learning Kotlin and wants to use this
project to learn it properly, whatever happens with the interview. Every piece of
code must teach as well as work. Treat "can Robert explain every line of this in the
follow-up interview?" as a requirement alongside passing the tests.

## Source of truth

- **API contract:** [src/main/resources/openapi/inventory.yaml](src/main/resources/openapi/inventory.yaml). Paths, status codes,
  content types and schemas must match it exactly. Error responses (400/404) are
  `text/plain` strings, not JSON. `quantity` in requests has `minimum: 1`.
- If the contract is ambiguous (e.g. malformed JSON, missing body, SKU id format),
  stop and ask Robert rather than guessing; record the decision in the README.

## Task list

[.claude/TODO.md](.claude/TODO.md) is the working task list. Read it at the start of each session,
check items off as they are done, and add new items as they come up. Its **oversell protection
test plan** is a hard requirement: a purchase must never oversell, even under concurrent requests.
Every feature that touches stock must add or extend tests from that plan.

## Stack

- Kotlin on the JVM, Spring Boot (Spring MVC), Gradle with the Kotlin DSL (`build.gradle.kts`).
  Chosen because it is what Nuuly runs in production.
- PostgreSQL (run with Docker Compose; Testcontainers in tests). Stock changes are single atomic
  SQL statements, backed by `CHECK (quantity >= 0)`. See the README decision record.
- Tests: JUnit 5 with Spring's test support.
- Open decisions are tracked in the README under "Open decisions". Do not settle
  one silently; propose it, explain the trade-offs, and let Robert choose.

## Documentation standard: clean code + study notes

The code reads like good production code. The teaching lives in a **study-notes file per
source file** under [docs/learning/notes/](docs/learning/notes/README.md) (the README there
has the path mapping and format).

**In the code:**

1. **KDoc on every non-private declaration**: classes, interfaces, objects, and functions.
   Keep it short: what it does and where it sits in the request flow
   (controller → service → repository). Use `@param`, `@return`, and `@throws` only when
   they add information. Test classes get a KDoc saying what they cover.
   A PostToolUse hook ([scripts/check_kdoc.py](scripts/check_kdoc.py)) enforces this mechanically.
2. **Inline comments only for decisions and contract rules**, one or two lines each:
   - `// Why:` a design decision and the alternative that was rejected.
   - `// Contract:` the line exists to satisfy a specific part of inventory.yaml.
3. **No teaching comments in code**: no `// Kotlin:` / `// Spring:` explanations, and no narration.
   Build files and `application.yml` may carry a one-line "what it's for" where it isn't obvious.

**In the notes** (`docs/learning/notes/<mirrored path>.md`):

4. Walk the file top to bottom in small chunks. **Quote each chunk** (don't reference line numbers)
   and explain it under `**Kotlin:**` (language features, with the Java equivalent when that
   helps), `**Spring:**` (framework behavior the code doesn't show), `**Why:**` and `**Contract:**`.
5. Explain a concept in full in the first notes file where it appears; elsewhere, link back to it.
   Index new concepts in [docs/learning/kotlin-concepts.md](docs/learning/kotlin-concepts.md).
6. End with "Check your understanding" questions, without answers.

**Keeping them in sync:** every code change updates its notes in the same piece of work. Run
`/sync-docs` to update them. A `Stop` hook ([scripts/check_notes.py](scripts/check_notes.py)) keeps
Claude working while any source file has changed more recently than its notes (or has none).

Use `/feature <description>` for any new behavior. It runs the whole loop:
contract check → plan (Robert approves) → tests + implementation → build →
`/sync-docs` (notes, concepts index, README, TODO, then the `doc-reviewer` agent) → hand-off to `/walkthrough`.

enough to explain and defend it in an interview. Go at his pace. This is a
conversation, not a lecture.

   **Wait for his reply before moving to the next file.** Don't answer your own question.
4. If his answer is wrong or partial, re-explain it another way. Don't just repeat the
   explanation.

1	# CLAUDE.md
2	
3	Project memory for Claude Code. Loaded automatically at the start of every session.
4	
5	## What this project is
6	
7	A take-home assessment for Nuuly: a small inventory REST API (receive stock by SKU,
8	process purchases, report inventory levels). Full brief: [docs/Nuuly_Assessment_Instructions.txt](docs/Nuuly_Assessment_Instructions.txt).
9	
10	**It is also a Kotlin master class.** Robert is learning Kotlin and wants to use this
11	project to learn it properly, whatever happens with the interview. Every piece of
12	code must teach as well as work. Treat "can Robert explain every line of this in the
13	follow-up interview?" as a requirement alongside passing the tests.
14	
15	## Source of truth
16	
17	- **API contract:** [src/main/resources/openapi/inventory.yaml](src/main/resources/openapi/inventory.yaml). Paths, status codes,
18	  content types and schemas must match it exactly. Error responses (400/404) are
19	  `text/plain` strings, not JSON. `quantity` in requests has `minimum: 1`.
20	- If the contract is ambiguous (e.g. malformed JSON, missing body, SKU id format),
21	  stop and ask Robert rather than guessing; record the decision in the README.
22	
23	## Task list
24	
25	[.claude/TODO.md](.claude/TODO.md) is the working task list. Read it at the start of each session,
26	check items off as they are done, and add new items as they come up. Its **oversell protection
27	test plan** is a hard requirement: a purchase must never oversell, even under concurrent requests.
28	Every feature that touches stock must add or extend tests from that plan.
29	
30	## Stack
31	
32	- Kotlin on the JVM, Spring Boot (Spring MVC), Gradle with the Kotlin DSL (`build.gradle.kts`).
33	  Chosen because it is what Nuuly runs in production.
34	- PostgreSQL (run with Docker Compose; Testcontainers in tests). Stock changes are single atomic
35	  SQL statements, backed by `CHECK (quantity >= 0)`. See the README decision record.
36	- Tests: JUnit 5 with Spring's test support.
37	- Open decisions are tracked in the README under "Open decisions". Do not settle
38	  one silently; propose it, explain the trade-offs, and let Robert choose.
39	
40	## Documentation standard: clean code + study notes
41	
42	The code reads like good production code. The teaching lives in a **study-notes file per
43	source file** under [docs/learning/notes/](docs/learning/notes/README.md) (the README there
44	has the path mapping and format).
45	
46	**In the code:**
47	
48	1. **KDoc on every non-private declaration**: classes, interfaces, objects, and functions.
49	   Keep it short: what it does and where it sits in the request flow
50	   (controller → service → repository). Use `@param`, `@return`, and `@throws` only when
51	   they add information. Test classes get a KDoc saying what they cover.
52	   A PostToolUse hook ([scripts/check_kdoc.py](scripts/check_kdoc.py)) enforces this mechanically.
53	2. **Inline comments only for decisions and contract rules**, one or two lines each:
54	   - `// Why:` a design decision and the alternative that was rejected.
55	   - `// Contract:` the line exists to satisfy a specific part of inventory.yaml.
56	3. **No teaching comments in code**: no `// Kotlin:` / `// Spring:` explanations, and no narration.
57	   Build files and `application.yml` may carry a one-line "what it's for" where it isn't obvious.
58	
59	**In the notes** (`docs/learning/notes/<mirrored path>.md`):
60	
61	1. Walk the file top to bottom in small chunks. **Quote each chunk** (don't reference line numbers)
62	   and explain it under `**Kotlin:**` (language features, with the Java equivalent when that
63	   helps), `**Spring:**` (framework behavior the code doesn't show), `**Why:**` and `**Contract:**`.
64	2. Explain a concept in full in the first notes file where it appears; elsewhere, link back to it.
65	   Index new concepts in [docs/learning/kotlin-concepts.md](docs/learning/kotlin-concepts.md).
66	3. End with "Check your understanding" questions, without answers.
67	
68	**Keeping them in sync:** every code change updates its notes in the same piece of work. Run
69	`/sync-docs` to update them. A `Stop` hook ([scripts/check_notes.py](scripts/check_notes.py)) keeps
70	Claude working while any source file has changed more recently than its notes (or has none).
71	
72	## Feature workflow
73	
74	Use `/feature <description>` for any new behavior. It runs the whole loop:
75	contract check → plan (Robert approves) → tests + implementation → build →
76	`/sync-docs` (notes, concepts index, README, TODO, then the `doc-reviewer` agent) → hand-off to `/walkthrough`.
77	For any other code change, run `/sync-docs` before handing the work back.
78	
79	- **Do not start the next feature until the walkthrough for the current one is done.**
80	- After the walkthrough, fix any comment that turned out to be unclear.
81	- Keep changes small and commit-sized. The reviewers want a readable, unsquashed
82	  git history. Propose a commit message, but only commit when Robert says so or runs `/ship`.
83	
84	## Git workflow: never work on main
85	
86	- **Every session starts on a new branch.** If the session starts on `main`, ask Robert what the
87	  session's work is before touching anything, then run
88	  `git switch main && git pull --ff-only && git switch -c <type>/<slug>`, where `<type>` is
89	  `feature`, `fix`, `chore`, `docs` or `test` (e.g. `feature/get-inventory`).
90	- One branch per piece of work. Commit in small, logical steps; the reviewers read the history.
91	- **`/ship`** is the only way work reaches `main`: push → PR → merge commit → back to an
92	  updated `main`. Never squash or rebase merges (the brief says "Do not squash commits").
93	- Enforced by `scripts/branch_guard.py`:
94	  - a `SessionStart` hook flags when the session starts on `main`
95	  - a `PreToolUse` hook blocks, while on `main`, edits to repo files and `git commit`/`git push`
96	  - on any branch, it blocks pushes to `main` and squash/rebase merges
97	
98	## Project tooling (.claude/)
99	
100	- `skills/feature/`: the `/feature` workflow above.
101	- `skills/walkthrough/`: `/walkthrough`, an interactive line-by-line teaching session
102	  on recent changes, logged to [docs/learning/walkthroughs/](docs/learning/walkthroughs/).
103	- `skills/ship/`: `/ship`, which pushes the current branch, opens a PR, and merges it into
104	  `main` with a merge commit. Build, test and review gates will be added later.
105	- `skills/sync-docs/`: `/sync-docs`, which updates study notes, the concepts index, the README
106	  and TODO for whatever code changed, then runs `doc-reviewer`.
107	- `agents/doc-reviewer.md`: read-only reviewer that checks changed code and its notes against
108	  the documentation standard above, accuracy first.
109	- `TODO.md`: the working task list.
110	- `settings.json` hooks:
111	  - `SessionStart` + `PreToolUse`: `scripts/branch_guard.py` (see Git workflow).
112	  - `Stop`: exports session transcripts to [docs/ai-sessions/](docs/ai-sessions/), and runs
113	    `scripts/check_notes.py` (stale or missing study notes send Claude back to `/sync-docs`).
114	  - `PostToolUse` (Edit/Write): runs `scripts/check_kdoc.py` on edited `.kt` files and
115	    reports missing KDoc back to Claude.
116	
117	## Environment
118	
119	Windows 11. Claude has PowerShell and Git Bash available. Python is on PATH and is
120	used for the hook scripts.
