-name: walkthrough

-description: Interactive teaching session that walks Robert through recently written code line by line, explaining Kotlin and Spring concepts, pausing for questions and checking understanding, then logs the session to docs/learning. Use after every feature, or when Robert asks to go through or explain code.
-argument-hint: "[optional: files, commit range, or topic; defaults to everything since the last walkthrough]"
-# /walkthrough $ARGUMENTS
-Robert is learning Kotlin through this project. He has to understand the code well
-enough to explain and defend it in an interview. Go at his pace. This is a
-conversation, not a lecture.
-## 1. Establish scope
-- If `$ARGUMENTS` names files, a commit range or a topic, use that.
-- Otherwise, find the last walkthrough log in `docs/learning/walkthroughs/` and read the
-  commit SHA it records. The scope is `<that sha>..HEAD` plus any uncommitted changes.
-  If there are no logs yet, the scope is everything under `src/` plus the build files.
-Show the list of files in scope. Order them along the path a request takes:
-build/config → entry point → controller → service → repository/model → error handling → tests.
-Ask whether that order works for him before starting.
-## 2. Walk through one file at a time
-For each file:
-1. **Role.** One or two sentences on what this file is for and how a request reaches it.
-2. **Code in small chunks** (roughly 5–20 lines). Quote each chunk with its `path:line` reference, then explain:
-   - every Kotlin feature in it: what it does, why it's idiomatic, and what the Java
-     equivalent would look like when that comparison helps;
-   - any Spring behavior that isn't visible in the code (what the framework does with the
-     annotation, when the object is created, what runs before and after);
-   - the design decision, and the alternative we rejected and why.
-3. **Pause.** Ask whether he has questions about the file. Then ask one short
-   check-your-understanding question, for example: "What happens if `quantity` is 0 here?"
-   or "Why is this a `val`?" or "What would the response be if the SKU doesn't exist?"
-   **Wait for his reply before moving to the next file.** Don't answer your own question.
-4. If his answer is wrong or partial, re-explain it another way. Don't just repeat the
-   explanation.
-5. If a question shows that a code comment is unclear or wrong, offer to fix the comment.
-Where a quick experiment would help, suggest one he can run himself, such as changing a
-value and rerunning a test to watch it fail, or a `curl` call against the running app.
-## 3. Wrap up
-- Recap the concepts covered in 3–6 bullets.
-- Ask whether anything should be revisited.
-## 4. Log it
-Write `docs/learning/walkthroughs/<YYYY-MM-DD>-<short-slug>.md` containing:
-# Walkthrough: <feature/topic>
-- Date: <date>
-- Covers: <first sha>..<HEAD sha> (plus uncommitted: yes/no)
-- Files: <list>
-## Concepts covered
-- <concept>: <one-line summary in Robert's terms>
-## Questions Robert asked
-## Understanding checks
-- <question> → <how he answered, what was clarified>
-## Follow-ups
-- <comments to fix, topics to revisit, exercises to try>
-Then update `docs/learning/kotlin-concepts.md`. For each concept seen for the first time, add a
-row with the concept, a short explanation, and a `path:line` link to where it first appears in
-this codebase. Don't add duplicate rows.

# Kotlin & Spring Concepts Index

A running index of every Kotlin and Spring concept used in this codebase. Each row links to
the study notes that explain it in full (see [notes/README.md](notes/README.md)). `/sync-docs`
and `/walkthrough` add rows as new concepts come up.

## Kotlin

| Concept | What it is | First seen |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Trailing lambdas / type-safe builders | A lambda passed last can sit outside `()`; Gradle's `plugins { }` blocks are function calls | [build.gradle.kts](notes/build.gradle.kts.md) |
| Final by default | Classes and functions are `final` unless `open`; the `plugin.spring` compiler plugin opens Spring beans | [build.gradle.kts](notes/build.gradle.kts.md) |
| Platform types and `-Xjsr305=strict` | How Java nullability annotations become real `T` / `T?` types | [build.gradle.kts](notes/build.gradle.kts.md) |
| Class with no body | `class InventoryApplication` needs no braces | [InventoryApplication.kt](notes/main/InventoryApplication.kt.md) |
| Top-level functions | `fun main` lives outside any class; compiled into `InventoryApplicationKt` | [InventoryApplication.kt](notes/main/InventoryApplication.kt.md) |
| Reified type parameters | `runApplication<T>()`, `withType<Test>`: the type in `<>` instead of `T::class.java` | [InventoryApplication.kt](notes/main/InventoryApplication.kt.md) |
| Infix functions | `a version b` means `a.version(b)` | [build.gradle.kts](notes/build.gradle.kts.md) |
| `Array<String>` | Kotlin's `String[]`: an ordinary generic class | [InventoryApplication.kt](notes/main/InventoryApplication.kt.md) |
| Spread operator `*` | Pass an array's elements as a vararg | [InventoryApplication.kt](notes/main/InventoryApplication.kt.md) |
| Named arguments | `proxyBeanMethods = false`, also in annotations | [TestcontainersConfiguration.kt](notes/test/support/TestcontainersConfiguration.kt.md) |
| Expression bodies | `fun f(): T = expr` instead of `{ return expr }` | [TestcontainersConfiguration.kt](notes/test/support/TestcontainersConfiguration.kt.md) |
| Class references `X::class` | Kotlin's version of Java's `X.class` | [InventoryApplicationTests.kt](notes/test/InventoryApplicationTests.kt.md) |
| `internal` vs package-private | Kotlin has no package-private; `internal` = same Gradle module | [README](../../README.md#project-layout) |

## Spring

| Concept | What it is | First seen |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `@SpringBootApplication` | `@Configuration` + `@EnableAutoConfiguration` + `@ComponentScan` from this package down | [InventoryApplication.kt](notes/main/InventoryApplication.kt.md) |
| Starters and the Boot BOM | Starters bundle dependencies; the dependency-management plugin supplies versions | [build.gradle.kts](notes/build.gradle.kts.md) |
| Docker Compose support | `bootRun` starts compose.yaml and wires the DataSource | [compose.yaml](notes/compose.yaml.md) |
| `@TestConfiguration` + `@Import` | Test-only beans that component scanning skips | [TestcontainersConfiguration.kt](notes/test/support/TestcontainersConfiguration.kt.md) |
| `@ServiceConnection` | A Testcontainers container supplies DataSource connection details | [TestcontainersConfiguration.kt](notes/test/support/TestcontainersConfiguration.kt.md) |
| `@SpringBootTest` | Starts the full application context in a test | [InventoryApplicationTests.kt](notes/test/InventoryApplicationTests.kt.md) |

-## Role
-The build definition: which compiler and plugins to use, which libraries the app and tests
-depend on, and how tests run. Generated by Spring Initializr (the command is in the commit
-"Generate the Spring Boot project with Spring Initializr") and then trimmed.
-## Walkthrough
-### The file is Kotlin: trailing lambdas
-```kotlin
-plugins {
-**Kotlin:** `plugins { ... }` is a *function call*. Its only argument is a lambda, and Kotlin
-lets a lambda that is the last argument move outside the parentheses. When it's the only
-argument, the parentheses disappear entirely. So `plugins { }` is really `plugins({ })`.
-Inside the lambda, `this` is a Gradle object (a "lambda with receiver"), which is why you can
-call `id(...)` or `kotlin(...)` without a prefix. This pattern is called a **type-safe builder**,
-and it's how Kotlin DSLs (Gradle, Ktor, kotlinx.html) read like configuration.
-### Plugins
-```kotlin
-kotlin("jvm") version "2.3.21"
-// Opens Spring-annotated classes: Kotlin classes are final by default, Spring needs to subclass some.
-kotlin("plugin.spring") version "2.3.21"
-id("org.springframework.boot") version "4.1.1"
-// Supplies versions from Spring Boot's BOM, so most dependencies below have none.
-id("io.spring.dependency-management") version "1.1.7"
-**Kotlin:** `kotlin("jvm")` is shorthand for `id("org.jetbrains.kotlin.jvm")`. `version` is an
-**infix function**: `a version b` means `a.version(b)`. Any single-argument function marked
-`infix` can be called that way.
-- **`kotlin("jvm")`**: runs the Kotlin compiler and targets the JVM.
-- **`kotlin("plugin.spring")`**: Kotlin classes and functions are **final by default** (Java is
-  the opposite; you have to write `final`). Spring sometimes creates a runtime *subclass* of
-  your bean (a proxy) to add behavior, e.g. `@Transactional` or `@Configuration`, and it can't
-  subclass a final class. This compiler plugin ("all-open") automatically makes classes with
-  Spring annotations `open`, so we don't have to write `open` everywhere.
-- **`org.springframework.boot`**: adds `bootRun` (run from source) and `bootJar` (one runnable
-  "fat" jar that contains all dependencies).
-- **`io.spring.dependency-management`**: imports Spring Boot's **BOM** (bill of materials), a
-  list of library versions tested together.
-**Why:** we have no version catalog (`libs.versions.toml`). The BOM already pins nearly every
-version, so a catalog would add indirection for no benefit.
-### Group, version and the Java toolchain
-```kotlin
-group = "com.robertwoolbright"
-version = "0.0.1-SNAPSHOT"
-java {
-    toolchain {
-        languageVersion = JavaLanguageVersion.of(21)
-**Kotlin:** `languageVersion = ...` looks like a field assignment. Gradle properties are lazy
-`Property<T>` objects, though, and Gradle's Kotlin DSL turns `=` into a call to `.set(...)`.
-Older builds write `languageVersion.set(JavaLanguageVersion.of(21))`.
-**Why:** a toolchain makes Gradle compile and test with JDK 21, whichever JDK is running Gradle
-itself (Gradle finds or downloads one). Anyone who clones the repo builds with the same Java
-version. The Kotlin plugin reads the toolchain too, so the bytecode targets Java 21.
-### Dependencies: configurations
-```kotlin
-dependencies {
-    implementation("org.springframework.boot:spring-boot-starter-flyway")
-    developmentOnly("org.springframework.boot:spring-boot-docker-compose")
-    runtimeOnly("org.postgresql:postgresql")
-    testImplementation(...)
-    testRuntimeOnly("org.junit.platform:junit-platform-launcher")
-The function name in front of each dependency (its *configuration*) decides where it's visible:
-| Configuration | Visible to |
-| `implementation` | app code at compile time and at runtime |
-| `runtimeOnly` | runtime only; our code never refers to it by name |
-| `developmentOnly` | `bootRun` only; left out of tests and of the jar |
-| `testImplementation` / `testRuntimeOnly` | the same idea, for `src/test` |
-**Spring:** a **starter** is a dependency that brings a coherent set of libraries plus the
-auto-configuration for them. Spring Boot 4 split the starters into smaller modules, which is why
-Flyway, JDBC and Web MVC each have their own starter and test starter.
-### App dependencies
-| Dependency | What it gives us |
-| `spring-boot-starter-flyway` | Runs the SQL migrations in `src/main/resources/db/migration` at startup, before any request is served. |
-| `flyway-database-postgresql` | Since Flyway 10, support for each database is a separate module. Without it, Flyway refuses to talk to Postgres. |
-| `spring-boot-starter-jdbc` | A pooled `DataSource` (HikariCP), `JdbcClient`/`JdbcTemplate` and a transaction manager, all auto-configured. `JdbcClient` is our data-access API. |
-| `spring-boot-starter-webmvc` | Spring MVC on an embedded Tomcat, plus Jackson for JSON. (Boot 4 renamed `starter-web` to `starter-webmvc`.) |
-| `kotlin-reflect` | Lets Spring read Kotlin metadata that Java reflection can't see, such as whether a parameter is nullable and whether it has a default value. |

-| `jackson-module-kotlin` | Teaches Jackson to build Kotlin classes. A `data class` has no no-arg constructor and no setters; this module calls the primary constructor and respects non-null types and default values. `tools.jackson` is **Jackson 3**'s group ID (Boot 4 moved to Jackson 3). |
-| `spring-boot-docker-compose` | On `bootRun`, runs `docker compose up` on `compose.yaml` and points the DataSource at it. See [compose.yaml notes](compose.yaml.md). |
-| `postgresql` | The JDBC driver. We code only against the standard `java.sql` interfaces, so it's `runtimeOnly`. |
-### Test dependencies
-| Dependency | What it gives us |

-| `spring-boot-starter-{flyway,jdbc,webmvc}-test` | Test support for each module, e.g. `@WebMvcTest` + `MockMvc` and `@JdbcTest`. They also pull in `spring-boot-starter-test`: JUnit 5, AssertJ, Mockito. |
-| `spring-boot-testcontainers` | `@ServiceConnection`, which turns a running container into DataSource settings. |
-| `kotlin-test-junit5` | `kotlin.test` assertions (`assertEquals`, `assertFailsWith`) backed by JUnit 5. |
-| `testcontainers-junit-jupiter`, `testcontainers-postgresql` | Start a real Postgres in Docker for tests. |
-| `junit-platform-launcher` | Gradle 9 no longer bundles the JUnit Platform launcher; it has to be on the test runtime classpath. |
-**Why:** tests run against real Postgres instead of H2, an in-memory database that imitates
-others. Our oversell protection depends on Postgres-specific behavior (`ON CONFLICT`, row locks
-during `UPDATE`, `CHECK` constraints), and H2 imitates those imperfectly.
-### Compiler options
-```kotlin
-kotlin {
-    compilerOptions {
-        freeCompilerArgs.addAll("-Xjsr305=strict", "-Xannotation-default-target=param-property")
-**Kotlin:** Kotlin's null safety (`String` can never be null; `String?` can) stops at the edge of
-Java code, because Java types carry no nullability. Kotlin treats an unannotated Java type as a
-**platform type**, shown as `String!`: you may treat it as nullable or not, and if you guess
-wrong you get a runtime NPE. Many Java libraries annotate their APIs instead.
-- **`-Xjsr305=strict`**: turns the JSR-305 annotations (`@Nonnull` / `@Nullable`) into real
-  `String` / `String?` types, so a mistake becomes a compile error. Spring Framework 7 uses the
-  newer JSpecify annotations, which Kotlin 2 already enforces; this flag covers libraries still
-  on JSR-305.
-- **`-Xannotation-default-target=param-property`**: in `class Q(@Ann val x: Int)`, the one
-  `val x` is a constructor parameter, a property and a backing field all at once, so an

+# compose.yaml
+> Source: [compose.yaml](../../../compose.yaml) · Last synced with code: 2026-09-23
+## Role
+Defines the Postgres container used when you run the app locally with `./gradlew bootRun`.
+Tests don't use it; they use Testcontainers (see
+[TestcontainersConfiguration notes](test/support/TestcontainersConfiguration.kt.md)).
+## Walkthrough
+### Who runs this file
+```yaml
+# Local Postgres for `./gradlew bootRun`. Spring Boot's Docker Compose support starts and stops
+# it automatically. Tests don't use this file; they use Testcontainers.
+**Spring:** you never run `docker compose up` yourself. The `spring-boot-docker-compose`
+dependency (`developmentOnly` in the build) finds `compose.yaml` at startup, starts it, and waits
+until the container is running and its mapped port accepts TCP connections. (That's Spring's
+default readiness check. It would use a compose `healthcheck` if we defined one.) It then reads the container's image, environment and mapped port
+and builds the DataSource connection details from them (a JDBC URL, user and password). On
+shutdown it stops the container. You can see this in the `bootRun` log: `Container ... Started`,
+then Flyway connecting to `jdbc:postgresql://127.0.0.1:<port>/inventory`.
+### Image version
+```yaml
+image: 'postgres:18'
+**Why:** pinned to a major version instead of `latest`, so a new Postgres major release can't
+change behavior without us noticing. `18` still receives the 18.x patch releases. Tests
+use the same tag, so local runs and tests behave the same.
+### Credentials
+```yaml
+environment:
+  - 'POSTGRES_DB=inventory'
+  - 'POSTGRES_USER=inventory'
+  - 'POSTGRES_PASSWORD=inventory'
+The official Postgres image creates this database and user on first start. These are throwaway,
+local-only values. Spring reads them from here, so they aren't repeated in `application.yml`.
+### Ports
+```yaml
+ports:
+  # Why: random free host port (no clash with a local Postgres), bound to 127.0.0.1 only so the
+  # dev database isn't reachable from the network. Plain '5432' would bind on all interfaces.
+The format is `host-ip:host-port:container-port`, and here the host port is left empty.
+**Why:** the host port is empty, so Docker picks a random free one (e.g. `53106`). A fixed
+`'5432:5432'` would fail if you already had Postgres running locally. Spring asks Docker which
+port it got, so nothing needs to know the number in advance.
+**Why `127.0.0.1`:** by default Docker publishes ports on *all* network interfaces. Other
+machines on your Wi-Fi could then reach a database whose password is `inventory`. Binding to
+the loopback address keeps it on this machine.
+## Check your understanding
+- If you run `docker compose up` yourself and then `bootRun`, what do you expect Spring to do?
+- Why doesn't `application.yml` need a `spring.datasource.url`?

15	```yaml
16	# Local Postgres for `./gradlew bootRun`. Spring Boot's Docker Compose support starts and stops
17	# it automatically. Tests don't use this file; they use Testcontainers.
18	```
19	
20	**Spring:** you never run `docker compose up` yourself. The `spring-boot-docker-compose`
21	dependency (`developmentOnly` in the build) finds `compose.yaml` at startup, starts it, and waits
22	until the container is running and its mapped port accepts TCP connections. (That's Spring's
23	default readiness check. It would use a compose `healthcheck` if we defined one.) It then reads the container's image, environment and mapped port
24	and builds the DataSource connection details from them (a JDBC URL, user and password). On
25	shutdown it stops the container. You can see this in the `bootRun` log: `Container ... Started`,
26	then Flyway connecting to `jdbc:postgresql://127.0.0.1:<port>/inventory`.
27	
28	### Image version
29	
30	```yaml
31	image: 'postgres:18'
32	```
33	
34	**Why:** pinned to a major version instead of `latest`, so a new Postgres major release can't
35	change behavior without us noticing. `18` still receives the 18.x patch releases. Tests
36	use the same tag, so local runs and tests behave the same.
37	
38	### Credentials
39	
40	```yaml
41	environment:
42	  - 'POSTGRES_DB=inventory'
43	  - 'POSTGRES_USER=inventory'
...
45	
46	The official Postgres image creates this database and user on first start. These are throwaway,
47	local-only values. Spring reads them from here, so they aren't repeated in `application.yml`.
48	
49	### Ports
50	
51	```yaml
52	ports:
53	  # Why: random free host port (no clash with a local Postgres), bound to 127.0.0.1 only so the
54	  # dev database isn't reachable from the network. Plain '5432' would bind on all interfaces.
55	  - '127.0.0.1::5432'
56	```
57	
58	The format is `host-ip:host-port:container-port`, and here the host port is left empty.
59	
60	**Why:** the host port is empty, so Docker picks a random free one (e.g. `53106`). A fixed
61	`'5432:5432'` would fail if you already had Postgres running locally. Spring asks Docker which
62	port it got, so nothing needs to know the number in advance.
63	
64	**Why `127.0.0.1`:** by default Docker publishes ports on *all* network interfaces. Other
65	machines on your Wi-Fi could then reach a database whose password is `inventory`. Binding to
66	the loopback address keeps it on this machine.
67	
68	## Check your understanding
69	
70	- If you run `docker compose up` yourself and then `bootRun`, what do you expect Spring to do?
71	- Why doesn't `application.yml` need a `spring.datasource.url`?

17	    ...
18	}
19	```

21	**Kotlin:** `plugins { ... }` is a *function call*. Its only argument is a lambda, and Kotlin
22	lets a lambda that is the last argument move outside the parentheses. When it's the only
23	argument, the parentheses disappear entirely. So `plugins { }` is really `plugins({ })`.

26	and it's how Kotlin DSLs (Gradle, Ktor, kotlinx.html) read like configuration.
27	
28	### Plugins
29	
30	```kotlin
31	kotlin("jvm") version "2.3.21"
32	// Opens Spring-annotated classes: Kotlin classes are final by default, Spring needs to subclass some.
33	kotlin("plugin.spring") version "2.3.21"
34	id("org.springframework.boot") version "4.1.1"
35	// Supplies versions from Spring Boot's BOM, so most dependencies below have none.
36	id("io.spring.dependency-management") version "1.1.7"
37	```
38	
39	**Kotlin:** `kotlin("jvm")` is shorthand for `id("org.jetbrains.kotlin.jvm")`. `version` is an
40	**infix function**: `a version b` means `a.version(b)`. Any single-argument function marked
41	`infix` can be called that way.

44	- **`kotlin("plugin.spring")`**: Kotlin classes and functions are **final by default** (Java is
45	  the opposite; you have to write `final`). Spring sometimes creates a runtime *subclass* of
46	  your bean (a proxy) to add behavior, e.g. `@Transactional` or `@Configuration`, and it can't
47	  subclass a final class. This compiler plugin ("all-open") automatically makes classes with
48	  Spring annotations `open`, so we don't have to write `open` everywhere.
49	- **`org.springframework.boot`**: adds `bootRun` (run from source) and `bootJar` (one runnable
50	  "fat" jar that contains all dependencies).
51	- **`io.spring.dependency-management`**: imports Spring Boot's **BOM** (bill of materials), a
52	  list of library versions tested together.

55	version, so a catalog would add indirection for no benefit.

61	version = "0.0.1-SNAPSHOT"

66	    }
67	}
68	```

92

lines: -name: doc-reviewer

-description: Read-only reviewer that checks changed Kotlin, Gradle, Spring config and SQL files and their study notes (docs/learning/notes/) against this project's documentation standard in CLAUDE.md. Accuracy comes first. Use after /sync-docs, after implementing a feature, and before a walkthrough.
-tools: Read, Grep, Glob, Bash
-You review a Kotlin + Spring Boot project that doubles as a Kotlin learning project for its
-author, Robert. The code is kept clean. The teaching lives in per-file study notes under
-`docs/learning/notes/`. Your job is to check whether someone new to Kotlin and Spring could
-understand every changed line from the code plus its notes, and whether everything the notes
-say is **true**.
-## Scope
-Unless the prompt names specific files, review what changed on this branch:
-`git diff --name-only main...HEAD` plus `git status --porcelain -uall`, limited to `*.kt`,

Everything is in place: the notes are in sync, the build passes, and `bootRun` works. The reviewer's second-pass items are fixed too, so the notes now pass both review passes.

## What changed

**The code is clean.** For example, [InventoryApplication.kt](src/main/kotlin/com/robertwoolbright/inventory/InventoryApplication.kt) is now 16 lines with short KDoc. Inline comments are now only one-line `// Why:` notes.

**The study notes live in [docs/learning/notes/](docs/learning/notes/README.md).** There's one notes file per source file. Each quotes its code a chunk at a time, explains it under **Kotlin / Spring / Why / Contract** headings, and ends with self-check questions.

**Three pieces keep the notes current:**

| Piece | What it does |
|---|---|
| [scripts/check_notes.py](scripts/check_notes.py) (`Stop` hook) | Claude can't end a turn while a source file has changed more recently than its notes, or has no notes. It also flags notes whose source file was deleted. It blocks at most once in a row, so it can't loop forever. |
| [/sync-docs](.claude/skills/sync-docs/SKILL.md) | Updates the notes, concepts index, README and TODO for whatever changed, then runs the reviewer until it passes. `/feature` now calls it. |
| [doc-reviewer](.claude/agents/doc-reviewer.md) | Now checks the notes: whether they're accurate, whether the quoted code still exists, and whether every chunk is covered. |

CLAUDE.md and `/walkthrough` are updated to match. `/walkthrough` now teaches from the notes and adds to them whenever you ask something they didn't cover.

## Mistakes the reviewer caught in my first draft

It found 7 real mistakes. Several would have taught you wrong things:
- **Spread operator:** I said `runApplication(args)` without `*` would pass the array as a single argument. It actually doesn't compile.
- **Named arguments:** I said Kotlin allows them in *any* call. They don't work for Java methods, and Java annotations *require* them for every parameter except `value`.
- **JUnit version:** Spring Boot 4 uses **JUnit 6**, not 5. I verified that in the resolved dependencies.
- It also caught a misstated compiler-flag rule, overstated test-context sharing, and a wrong readiness check.
- **Security fix:** Docker was publishing the dev Postgres port on every network interface. It's now bound to `127.0.0.1` only. I confirmed `bootRun` still works with the new binding.

## Commits

Nothing is committed yet. I'd split the work into two commits:

1. `Move teaching comments into per-file study notes`: the slimmed code, the notes, the docs, the JUnit 6 corrections and the loopback port binding.
2. `Keep study notes in sync with code`: the `check_notes.py` hook, `/sync-docs`, and the `doc-reviewer`, `/feature` and `/walkthrough` updates.

Should I commit these? Then we can restart `/walkthrough` from `settings.gradle.kts`, this time working from the notes.

"""Stop hook: every source file must have study notes that are at least as new as the code.

The code carries only short KDoc and one-line `// Why:` / `// Contract:` comments. The teaching
lives in docs/learning/notes/, one Markdown file per source file (see the README there for the
mapping). This hook keeps the two from drifting apart.

Claude Code runs it when Claude is about to end its turn (see .claude/settings.json). For each
source file it compares "when did this last change" for the file and for its notes:

  - a file with uncommitted changes (modified, staged or untracked): its modification time
  - a committed, unchanged file: the time of the last commit that touched it

If the code is newer than its notes, or the notes are missing, the script prints what's stale to
stderr and exits 2. Claude Code then keeps Claude working with that message as feedback, and
Claude runs /sync-docs. It also reports notes whose source file no longer exists.

To avoid an endless loop, it never blocks twice in a row: when Claude Code says a Stop hook
already sent Claude back to work (`stop_hook_active`), the script lets the turn end.

# /walkthrough the project scaffold: settings.gradle.kts, build.gradle.kts, compose.yaml, application.yml, InventoryApplication.kt, TestcontainersConfiguration.kt, InventoryApplicationTests.kt

Robert is learning Kotlin through this project. He has to understand the code well
enough to explain and defend it in an interview. Go at his pace. This is a
conversation, not a lecture.

## 1. Establish scope

- If `the project scaffold: settings.gradle.kts, build.gradle.kts, compose.yaml, application.yml, InventoryApplication.kt, TestcontainersConfiguration.kt, InventoryApplicationTests.kt` names files, a commit range or a topic, use that.
- Otherwise, find the last walkthrough log in `docs/learning/walkthroughs/` and read the
  commit SHA it records. The scope is `<that sha>..HEAD` plus any uncommitted changes.
  If there are no logs yet, the scope is everything under `src/` plus the build files.

Show the list of files in scope. Order them along the path a request takes:
build/config → entry point → controller → service → repository/model → error handling → tests.
Ask whether that order works for him before starting.

## 2. Walk through one file at a time

Each source file has a study-notes file in `docs/learning/notes/` (mapping in its README).
Read the source and its notes first, and use the notes as your script: they hold the
explanations and the check-your-understanding questions. If the notes are missing or don't
match the code, run `/sync-docs` before starting.

For each file:

1. **Role.** One or two sentences on what this file is for and how a request reaches it.
2. **Code in small chunks** (roughly 5–20 lines), following the notes' sections. Quote each chunk with its `path:line` reference, then explain:
   - every Kotlin feature in it: what it does, why it's idiomatic, and what the Java
     equivalent would look like when that comparison helps;
   - any Spring behavior that isn't visible in the code (what the framework does with the
     annotation, when the object is created, what runs before and after);
   - the design decision, and the alternative we rejected and why.
3. **Pause.** Ask whether he has questions about the file. Then ask one short
   check-your-understanding question, for example: "What happens if `quantity` is 0 here?"
   or "Why is this a `val`?" or "What would the response be if the SKU doesn't exist?"
   **Wait for his reply before moving to the next file.** Don't answer your own question.
4. If his answer is wrong or partial, re-explain it another way. Don't just repeat the
   explanation.
5. If a question shows that a note or code comment is unclear or wrong, offer to fix it. Add

Where a quick experiment would help, suggest one he can run himself, such as changing a
value and rerunning a test to watch it fail, or a `curl` call against the running app.

## 3. Wrap up

- Recap the concepts covered in 3–6 bullets.
- Ask whether anything should be revisited.

Write `docs/learning/walkthroughs/<YYYY-MM-DD>-<short-slug>.md` containing:

## 1. settings.gradle.kts

**Role:** Gradle has two kinds of build file. The *settings* file decides which projects are in the build. The *build* file (next) decides how each project is built. Gradle reads this one first.

[settings.gradle.kts:1-2](settings.gradle.kts#L1-L2)
```kotlin
// Study notes: docs/learning/notes/settings.gradle.kts.md
rootProject.name = "inventory"
```

- **`.kts` means Kotlin script.** The file is real Kotlin, compiled and type-checked. Put a typo in `name` and the IDE underlines it before you run anything. Older Gradle builds use Groovy (`settings.gradle`), which is dynamically typed and only fails when it runs.
- **`rootProject.name = ...`** looks like assigning a variable, but you're setting a property on an object Gradle gives you. Inside a settings script, `this` is a Gradle `Settings` object, and `rootProject` is one of its properties. We'll see this idea again in `build.gradle.kts` as the "lambda with receiver".
- **What the name affects:** Gradle's display name, and the jar file name, `build/libs/inventory-0.0.1-SNAPSHOT.jar`. The `0.0.1-SNAPSHOT` part comes from `build.gradle.kts`.
- **Why a single module:** a multi-module build (`api/`, `domain/`, …) would list its modules here with `include(...)`. We decided four endpoints don't justify that.

content.text:
Correct. It would be:

```kotlin

include("api", "domain")
```

To finish the picture: each module then gets its own folder with its own `build.gradle.kts`, and the root `build.gradle.kts` usually shrinks to settings they share. The settings file lists the modules, and each module's build file describes how that module is built.

---

## 2. build.gradle.kts

**Role:** the build definition. It says which compiler and plugins to use, which libraries the app and tests need, and how tests run. It's also the most Kotlin-heavy file we have, so we'll take it in three parts. Part 1 is below.

### Part 1a: the whole file is function calls

[build.gradle.kts:2-9](build.gradle.kts#L2-L9)
```kotlin
plugins {
    kotlin("jvm") version "2.3.21"
    // Opens Spring-annotated classes: Kotlin classes are final by default, Spring needs to subclass some.
    kotlin("plugin.spring") version "2.3.21"
    id("org.springframework.boot") version "4.1.1"
    // Supplies versions from Spring Boot's BOM, so most dependencies below have none.
    id("io.spring.dependency-management") version "1.1.7"
}
```

**Kotlin: trailing lambdas.** `plugins { ... }` looks like a config block, but it's a **function call** whose only argument is a lambda (a block of code passed as a value). Kotlin has two rules here:
1. If the last argument is a lambda, it can move outside the parentheses: `plugins() { ... }`.
2. If it's the *only* argument, the empty `()` can go too: `plugins { ... }`.

So `plugins { ... }` is `plugins({ ... })`. In Java you'd write something like `plugins(spec -> { ... })`.

**Kotlin: lambda with receiver.** Inside the braces you call `id(...)` and `kotlin(...)` with no object in front. That's because Gradle runs the lambda with `this` set to a plugins-configuration object, and `id(...)` really means `this.id(...)`. A block like this, where the braces decide what `this` is, is called a **type-safe builder**. It's how Kotlin DSLs read like configuration while staying type-checked.

**Kotlin: infix functions.** `id("...") version "4.1.1"` is `id("...").version("4.1.1")`. A single-argument function marked `infix` can drop the dot and parentheses. `kotlin("jvm")` is just shorthand for `id("org.jetbrains.kotlin.jvm")`.

**What each plugin does:**
- **`kotlin("jvm")`**: compiles Kotlin to JVM bytecode.
- **`plugin.spring`**: this one matters most. Kotlin classes are **final by default**, the opposite of Java. Spring sometimes creates a *subclass* of your bean at runtime (a proxy) to wrap extra behavior around your methods, for example to begin and commit a transaction. You can't subclass a final class. This compiler plugin automatically marks classes with Spring annotations as `open`.
- **`org.springframework.boot`**: adds the `bootRun` and `bootJar` tasks.
- **`dependency-management`**: loads Spring Boot's BOM (bill of materials), a list of library versions tested together. That's why most dependencies further down have no version.

### Part 1b: coordinates, Java version, repositories

[build.gradle.kts:11-22](build.gradle.kts#L11-L22)
```kotlin
group = "com.robertwoolbright"
version = "0.0.1-SNAPSHOT"

java {
    toolchain {
        languageVersion = JavaLanguageVersion.of(21)
    }
}

repositories {
    mavenCentral()
}
```

- **`group` / `version`** are the project's Maven coordinates. `version` ends up in the jar name, and `SNAPSHOT` is the Maven convention for "work in progress, not a release".
- **`java { toolchain { ... } }`**: nested builders, same pattern as before. **Why:** the toolchain makes Gradle compile and test with JDK 21 *regardless of which JDK is running Gradle*. A reviewer with Java 17 as their default still builds with 21. Gradle finds one, or downloads it.
- **Kotlin + Gradle:** `languageVersion = ...` looks like setting a field, but `languageVersion` is a lazy Gradle `Property<T>`. Gradle's Kotlin DSL turns `=` into `.set(...)`. You'll see `languageVersion.set(JavaLanguageVersion.of(21))` in older builds.
- **`mavenCentral()`**: where dependencies are downloaded from.

---

**Any questions on part 1?**

**Check your understanding:** Suppose we removed `kotlin("plugin.spring")` from the build. Later we add a `@Service` class with a `@Transactional` method. What goes wrong, and why wouldn't it happen in Java?

Well in Java everything by default is open vs Kotlin which is final. 
When we have more complicated behaviours around meathods Spring creates subclasses, but you cannot create a subclass of a final class as it is immutable. 
the plugin.spring automaticaly marks classes with spring annotations as open. 
So in your example if it was removed it would stay final and not be open. The more complex behaviours a transactional flow requires and the changing of the values in the class would not be able to happen in a final class in Kotlin. 

Java it would all be open so it would be fine.

You've got the main idea: Kotlin is final by default, Java is open by default, Spring needs to subclass, and `plugin.spring` bridges the gap. One piece needs correcting, though, because it's a common mix-up and interviewers probe it:

**`final` doesn't mean immutable.** They're two separate ideas:

| | Controls | Kotlin keyword |
|---|---|---|
| **final / open** | whether a class can be *subclassed*, or a method *overridden* | `open` (final is the default) |
| **mutable / immutable** | whether a *value* can change after it's set | `var` vs `val` |

A final class can hold perfectly mutable state:

```kotlin
class Counter {          // final: nobody can subclass it
    var count = 0        // but count can change freely
}
```

The Spring proxy also doesn't change any values in your class. It **wraps method calls**. Picture what Spring generates at runtime, roughly:

```kotlin
class InventoryService$$Proxy : InventoryService() {      // subclass: needs InventoryService to be open
    override fun purchase(...) {                          // override: needs purchase() to be open too
        beginTransaction()
        try { super.purchase(...); commit() }
        catch (e: Exception) { rollback(); throw e }
    }
}
```

That shows the other half of the problem: **methods are final by default too**, and the plugin opens those as well. Without the plugin, what goes wrong depends on what's final:
- **The class is final:** Spring fails *at startup* with an error like "Cannot subclass final class". That's loud and easy to find.
- **The class is open but the method is final:** Spring can create the subclass but can't override the method, so your code runs **without a transaction and without any error**. That's the dangerous case.

You were right about Java: everything is open there, so this never comes up.

I'm adding the final-vs-immutable distinction and the silent-failure case to the build notes, since the notes didn't cover them.

# build.gradle.kts

> Source: [build.gradle.kts](../../../build.gradle.kts) · Last synced with code: 2026-09-23

## Role

The build definition: which compiler and plugins to use, which libraries the app and tests
depend on, and how tests run. Generated by Spring Initializr (the command is in the commit
"Generate the Spring Boot project with Spring Initializr") and then trimmed.

## Walkthrough

### The file is Kotlin: trailing lambdas

```kotlin
plugins {
    ...
}
```

**Kotlin:** `plugins { ... }` is a *function call*. Its only argument is a lambda, and Kotlin
lets a lambda that is the last argument move outside the parentheses. When it's the only
argument, the parentheses disappear entirely. So `plugins { }` is really `plugins({ })`.
Inside the lambda, `this` is a Gradle object (a "lambda with receiver"), which is why you can
call `id(...)` or `kotlin(...)` without a prefix. This pattern is called a **type-safe builder**,
and it's how Kotlin DSLs (Gradle, Ktor, kotlinx.html) read like configuration.

### Plugins

```kotlin
kotlin("jvm") version "2.3.21"
// Opens Spring-annotated classes: Kotlin classes are final by default, Spring needs to subclass some.
kotlin("plugin.spring") version "2.3.21"
id("org.springframework.boot") version "4.1.1"
// Supplies versions from Spring Boot's BOM, so most dependencies below have none.
id("io.spring.dependency-management") version "1.1.7"
```

**Kotlin:** `kotlin("jvm")` is shorthand for `id("org.jetbrains.kotlin.jvm")`. `version` is an
**infix function**: `a version b` means `a.version(b)`. Any single-argument function marked
`infix` can be called that way.

- **`kotlin("jvm")`**: runs the Kotlin compiler and targets the JVM.
- **`kotlin("plugin.spring")`**: Kotlin classes and functions are **final by default** (Java is
  the opposite; you have to write `final`). Spring sometimes creates a runtime *subclass* of
  your bean (a proxy) to add behavior, e.g. `@Transactional` or `@Configuration`, and it can't
  subclass a final class. This compiler plugin ("all-open") automatically makes classes with
  Spring annotations `open`, so we don't have to write `open` everywhere.
- **`org.springframework.boot`**: adds `bootRun` (run from source) and `bootJar` (one runnable
  "fat" jar that contains all dependencies).
- **`io.spring.dependency-management`**: imports Spring Boot's **BOM** (bill of materials), a
  list of library versions tested together.

**Why:** we have no version catalog (`libs.versions.toml`). The BOM already pins nearly every
version, so a catalog would add indirection for no benefit.

### Group, version and the Java toolchain

```kotlin
group = "com.robertwoolbright"
version = "0.0.1-SNAPSHOT"

java {
    toolchain {
        languageVersion = JavaLanguageVersion.of(21)
    }
}
```

`group` and `version` are the project's Maven coordinates. They would identify the artifact
if we published it, and `version` ends up in the jar name. `SNAPSHOT` is the Maven convention for
"work in progress, not a release".

**Kotlin:** `languageVersion = ...` looks like a field assignment. Gradle properties are lazy
`Property<T>` objects, though, and Gradle's Kotlin DSL turns `=` into a call to `.set(...)`.
Older builds write `languageVersion.set(JavaLanguageVersion.of(21))`.

**Why:** a toolchain makes Gradle compile and test with JDK 21, whichever JDK is running Gradle
itself (Gradle finds or downloads one). Anyone who clones the repo builds with the same Java
version. The Kotlin plugin reads the toolchain too, so the bytecode targets Java 21.

### Repositories

```kotlin
repositories {
    mavenCentral()
}
```

Where Gradle downloads dependencies from. Maven Central is the main public repository for JVM
libraries; everything we use is published there.

### Dependencies: configurations

```kotlin
dependencies {
    implementation("org.springframework.boot:spring-boot-starter-flyway")
    ...
    developmentOnly("org.springframework.boot:spring-boot-docker-compose")
    runtimeOnly("org.postgresql:postgresql")
    testImplementation(...)
    testRuntimeOnly("org.junit.platform:junit-platform-launcher")
}
```

The function name in front of each dependency (its *configuration*) decides where it's visible:

| Configuration | Visible to |
| --- | --- |
| `implementation` | app code at compile time and at runtime |
| `runtimeOnly` | runtime only; our code never refers to it by name |
| `developmentOnly` | `bootRun` only; left out of tests and of the jar |
| `testImplementation` / `testRuntimeOnly` | the same idea, for `src/test` |

**Spring:** a **starter** is a dependency that brings a coherent set of libraries plus the
auto-configuration for them. Spring Boot 4 split the starters into smaller modules, which is why
Flyway, JDBC and Web MVC each have their own starter and test starter.

### App dependencies

| Dependency | What it gives us |
| --- | --- |
| `spring-boot-starter-flyway` | Runs the SQL migrations in `src/main/resources/db/migration` at startup, before any request is served. |
| `flyway-database-postgresql` | Since Flyway 10, support for most databases, Postgres included, is a separate module. Without it, Flyway refuses to talk to Postgres. |
| `spring-boot-starter-jdbc` | A pooled `DataSource` (HikariCP), `JdbcClient`/`JdbcTemplate` and a transaction manager, all auto-configured. `JdbcClient` is our data-access API. |
| `spring-boot-starter-webmvc` | Spring MVC on an embedded Tomcat, plus Jackson for JSON. (Boot 4 introduced `starter-webmvc`; the old `starter-web` still exists but is deprecated.) |
| `kotlin-reflect` | Lets Spring read Kotlin metadata that Java reflection can't see, such as whether a parameter is nullable and whether it has a default value. |
| `jackson-module-kotlin` | Teaches Jackson to build Kotlin classes. A `data class` with `val` properties has no no-arg constructor and no setters; this module calls the primary constructor and respects non-null types and default values. `tools.jackson` is **Jackson 3**'s group ID (Boot 4 moved to Jackson 3). |
| `spring-boot-docker-compose` | On `bootRun`, runs `docker compose up` on `compose.yaml` and points the DataSource at it. See [compose.yaml notes](compose.yaml.md). |
| `postgresql` | The JDBC driver. We code only against the standard `java.sql` interfaces, so it's `runtimeOnly`. |

### Test dependencies

| Dependency | What it gives us |
| --- | --- |
| `spring-boot-starter-{flyway,jdbc,webmvc}-test` | Test support for each module, e.g. `@WebMvcTest` + `MockMvc` and `@JdbcTest`. They also pull in `spring-boot-starter-test`: JUnit Jupiter 6, AssertJ, Mockito. |
| `spring-boot-testcontainers` | `@ServiceConnection`, which turns a running container into DataSource settings. |
| `kotlin-test-junit5` | `kotlin.test` assertions (`assertEquals`, `assertFailsWith`) backed by JUnit Jupiter. The artifact keeps its old `junit5` name, but it runs fine on JUnit 6. |
| `testcontainers-junit-jupiter`, `testcontainers-postgresql` | Start a real Postgres in Docker for tests. |
| `junit-platform-launcher` | Gradle 9 no longer bundles the JUnit Platform launcher; it has to be on the test runtime classpath. |

**Why:** tests run against real Postgres instead of H2, an in-memory database that imitates
others. Our oversell protection depends on Postgres-specific behavior (`ON CONFLICT`, row locks
during `UPDATE`, `CHECK` constraints), and H2 imitates those imperfectly.

### Compiler options

```kotlin
kotlin {
    compilerOptions {
        freeCompilerArgs.addAll("-Xjsr305=strict", "-Xannotation-default-target=param-property")
    }
}
```

**Kotlin:** Kotlin's null safety (`String` can never be null; `String?` can) stops at the edge of
Java code, because Java types carry no nullability. Kotlin treats an unannotated Java type as a
**platform type**, shown as `String!`: you may treat it as nullable or not, and if you guess
wrong you get a runtime NPE. Many Java libraries annotate their APIs instead.
- **`-Xjsr305=strict`**: turns the JSR-305 annotations (`@Nonnull` / `@Nullable`) into real
  `String` / `String?` types, so a mistake becomes a compile error. Spring Framework 7 uses the
  newer JSpecify annotations, which Kotlin 2.1+ enforces by default; this flag covers libraries still
  on JSR-305.
- **`-Xannotation-default-target=param-property`**: in `class Q(@Ann val x: Int)`, the one
  `val x` is a constructor parameter, a property and a backing field all at once, so an
  annotation on it is ambiguous. This option puts it on the parameter, **and** on the property
  if the annotation is allowed to target a property; otherwise on the backing field. Java
  annotations such as `@NotBlank` or `@JsonProperty` can't target a Kotlin property, so they land
  on the parameter and the field. Those are the places Bean Validation and Jackson look.
  This will become Kotlin's default in a future release.

### Tests run on the JUnit Platform

```kotlin
tasks.withType<Test> {
    useJUnitPlatform()
}
```

Spring Boot 4 manages **JUnit 6**. The test API we write against (`org.junit.jupiter.api.Test`)
is the same Jupiter API as JUnit 5. `useJUnitPlatform()` tells Gradle to run tests through the
JUnit Platform rather than the legacy JUnit 4 runner.

**Kotlin:** `withType<Test>` uses a **reified type parameter**. On the JVM, generic types are
normally erased at runtime, but an `inline` function can mark its type parameter `reified` and
use it as a real class. So you write `withType<Test>` instead of Java's
`withType(Test.class)`. The trailing lambda then configures every `Test` task.

content.text:
### Part 2a: app dependencies

[build.gradle.kts:24-32](build.gradle.kts#L24-L32)
```kotlin
dependencies {
    implementation("org.springframework.boot:spring-boot-starter-flyway")
    implementation("org.flywaydb:flyway-database-postgresql")
    implementation("org.springframework.boot:spring-boot-starter-jdbc")
    implementation("org.springframework.boot:spring-boot-starter-webmvc")
    implementation("org.jetbrains.kotlin:kotlin-reflect")
    implementation("tools.jackson.module:jackson-module-kotlin")
    developmentOnly("org.springframework.boot:spring-boot-docker-compose")
    runtimeOnly("org.postgresql:postgresql")
```

**The function name is the important part.** `implementation`, `runtimeOnly` and so on are *configurations*: they decide where a library is visible.

| Configuration | Visible to |
|---|---|
| `implementation` | your code, at compile time and at runtime |
| `runtimeOnly` | runtime only; your code can't even refer to it |
| `developmentOnly` | `bootRun` only; not in tests, not in the jar |

**Spring: starters.** A *starter* is one dependency that pulls in a set of libraries that belong together, plus Spring's auto-configuration for them. Add `starter-jdbc` and, without writing any code, you get a connection pool, `JdbcClient` and a transaction manager.

What each line gives us:
- **`starter-flyway` + `flyway-database-postgresql`**: runs our SQL migrations at startup. Since Flyway 10, Postgres support is a separate module, and without it Flyway refuses to connect.
- **`starter-jdbc`**: the connection pool, plus `JdbcClient`, the data-access API we chose.
- **`starter-webmvc`**: Spring MVC on an embedded Tomcat, plus Jackson for JSON.
- **`kotlin-reflect`**: lets Spring read things only Kotlin knows about, like "is this parameter nullable?" and "does it have a default value?".
- **`jackson-module-kotlin`**: this matters when we write `data class QuantityRequest(val quantity: Int)`. Plain Jackson builds an object by calling a no-arg constructor and then calling setters. Our data class has neither, because `val` means no setter. This module makes Jackson call the constructor with the JSON values instead.
- **`spring-boot-docker-compose`**: starts `compose.yaml` on `bootRun`. `developmentOnly` keeps it out of the production jar, which should never try to start Docker.
- **`postgresql`** (the JDBC driver): `runtimeOnly`, because our code only uses the standard `java.sql` interfaces and never names a Postgres class.

### Part 2b: test dependencies

[build.gradle.kts:34-43](build.gradle.kts#L34-L43)
```kotlin
    testImplementation("org.springframework.boot:spring-boot-starter-flyway-test")
    testImplementation("org.springframework.boot:spring-boot-starter-jdbc-test")
    testImplementation("org.springframework.boot:spring-boot-starter-webmvc-test")
    testImplementation("org.springframework.boot:spring-boot-testcontainers")
    testImplementation("org.jetbrains.kotlin:kotlin-test-junit5")
    // Why: tests run against real Postgres, not H2; oversell protection depends on Postgres behavior.
    testImplementation("org.testcontainers:testcontainers-junit-jupiter")
    testImplementation("org.testcontainers:testcontainers-postgresql")
    testRuntimeOnly("org.junit.platform:junit-platform-launcher")
}
```

- **The `-test` starters** give each module its test tools. For example, `webmvc-test` gives us `MockMvc` for testing controllers without a real server. Together they also bring in JUnit (version 6 in Boot 4), AssertJ and Mockito.
- **`spring-boot-testcontainers`**: provides `@ServiceConnection`, which we'll see in file 6.
- **`kotlin-test-junit5`**: Kotlin-flavored assertions such as `assertEquals` and `assertFailsWith<SomeException> { ... }`.
- **The Testcontainers pair**: a real Postgres in Docker for every test run.
- **`junit-platform-launcher`**: Gradle 9 needs it on the test runtime classpath to start JUnit.

**Why real Postgres instead of H2** (the `// Why:` line): H2 is an in-memory database that imitates others. Our no-oversell guarantee depends on exact Postgres behavior: `INSERT ... ON CONFLICT`, row locking during a conditional `UPDATE`, and `CHECK` constraints. If a test passes on an imitation, it proves little about production.

---

**Any questions on part 2?**

**Check your understanding:** `postgresql` is `runtimeOnly`. What would happen if you wrote `import org.postgresql.PGConnection` in one of our Kotlin files: would it compile, would it run, or neither?

We would get a dependency issue. Our code uses the standard java sql. 
So we dont deal with posgres classes

Right direction, but "a dependency issue" is vague, and an interviewer will push for the specifics. Here they are.

Gradle keeps **two separate classpaths** (lists of libraries it can see) for your code:

```
                         compile classpath    runtime classpath
implementation              ✅                   ✅
runtimeOnly                 ❌                   ✅
compileOnly                 ✅                   ❌
```

So the answer is: **it fails to compile.** The Kotlin compiler never sees the Postgres jar and reports `Unresolved reference: postgresql` on the import. It never gets as far as running, even though the jar *would* be present at runtime.

That's also why `runtimeOnly` is useful and not just tidy. It **enforces** the design you described: "our code uses standard `java.sql`, not Postgres classes." If someone ever adds Postgres-specific code, the build fails right away. The fix would be a deliberate change to `implementation`, which makes the new dependency visible in code review.

`compileOnly` is the mirror image. It compiles fine but crashes at runtime with `NoClassDefFoundError`. You use it for things the runtime environment provides.

---

### Part 3a: compiler options

[build.gradle.kts:45-49](build.gradle.kts#L45-L49)
```kotlin
kotlin {
    compilerOptions {
        freeCompilerArgs.addAll("-Xjsr305=strict", "-Xannotation-default-target=param-property")
    }
}
```

**Kotlin: platform types.** Kotlin's null safety works like this: `String` can never be null, and `String?` can. The compiler forces you to handle the `?` case. But Kotlin calls a lot of Java code, and plain Java types don't say whether they can be null. Kotlin calls those **platform types**, shown as `String!`. It lets you treat one either way, and if you guess wrong you get a `NullPointerException` at runtime, just like Java.

Many Java libraries annotate their methods with `@Nullable` or `@NonNull`.

**`-Xjsr305=strict`** tells Kotlin to *trust* those annotations completely. A Java method marked `@Nullable String find()` becomes `String?` in Kotlin, so forgetting the null check is a **compile error** rather than a runtime crash. (Spring 7 uses a newer annotation style, JSpecify, that Kotlin 2.1+ already treats strictly. This flag covers libraries still using the older style.)

**`-Xannotation-default-target=param-property`** matters later, for request bodies. In Kotlin, one line like

```kotlin
data class QuantityRequest(@Min(1) val quantity: Int)
```

That's correct, and well put.

One detail to sharpen it. Without the flag, Kotlin's default for these annotations is **warn**: you get a compiler *warning* (which is easy to scroll past), the code builds, and it throws the `NullPointerException` at runtime if the value really is null. The flag turns that warning into an error that stops the build.

Once it's an error, the fix is idiomatic Kotlin you'll use all over this project:

```kotlin
val len = result?.length ?: 0
```

`?.` means "call this only if `result` isn't null, otherwise the whole expression is null". `?:` (the "Elvis operator") means "if the left side is null, use this value instead". We'll cover both properly when they show up in real code.

## 3. compose.yaml

**Role:** defines the Postgres container used by `./gradlew bootRun`. It isn't Kotlin, but there's Spring behavior hidden in it. Tests don't use this file.

[compose.yaml:1-8](compose.yaml#L1-L8)
```yaml
# Study notes: docs/learning/notes/compose.yaml.md
# Local Postgres for `./gradlew bootRun`. Spring Boot's Docker Compose support starts and stops
# it automatically. Tests don't use this file; they use Testcontainers.
services:
  postgres:
    # Why: pinned major version, kept in sync with support/TestcontainersConfiguration.kt.
    image: 'postgres:18'
```

**Spring: you never run Docker yourself.** When you run `bootRun`, the `spring-boot-docker-compose` dependency does this in order:
1. finds `compose.yaml` and runs `docker compose up`;
2. waits until the container's port accepts connections;
3. **recognizes the service by its image** (`postgres`), so it knows this is a Postgres database;
4. builds the database connection details (JDBC URL, user, password) from this file;
5. on shutdown, stops the container. It only stops what it started: if you had already started the services yourself, they stay running.

The service name `postgres:` is only a label. Spring goes by the image, not the name.

**Why `postgres:18` and not `latest`:** `latest` silently becomes Postgres 19 when that's released. Pinning the major version still gets you 18.x bug fixes, but no surprise behavior changes. The test container uses the same tag, so local runs and tests match.

[compose.yaml:9-16](compose.yaml#L9-L16)
```yaml
    environment:
      - 'POSTGRES_DB=inventory'
      - 'POSTGRES_USER=inventory'
      - 'POSTGRES_PASSWORD=inventory'
    ports:
      # Why: random free host port (no clash with a local Postgres), bound to 127.0.0.1 only so the
      # dev database isn't reachable from the network. Plain '5432' would bind on all interfaces.
      - '127.0.0.1::5432'
```

- **`environment`**: the official Postgres image creates this database and user when it first starts. Spring reads the same values from here, which is why none of them are repeated in `application.yml`.
- **`'127.0.0.1::5432'`** has the format `host-ip : host-port : container-port`, with the middle part left empty:
  - **Empty host port:** Docker picks a random free port (last run it was `54510`). A fixed `5432:5432` would fail if you already had Postgres installed. Spring asks Docker which port it got, so nothing needs to know the number in advance.
  - **`127.0.0.1`:** by default Docker publishes on *every* network interface, so anyone on your Wi-Fi could connect with password `inventory`. Binding to the loopback address keeps it on your machine. This was the reviewer's security catch from earlier.

**Try it yourself:** run `./gradlew bootRun`. In another terminal, run `docker ps` and look at the PORTS column. You'll see `127.0.0.1:<random>->5432/tcp`, and the same port appears in the Flyway log line. Press Ctrl+C and run `docker ps` again: the container is gone.

## 4. application.yml

**Role:** Spring Boot's configuration file. Spring loads it automatically from the classpath at startup, and any setting it doesn't mention keeps its auto-configured default.

[application.yml:1-6](src/main/resources/application.yml#L1-L6)
```yaml
# Study notes: docs/learning/notes/main/resources/application.yml.md
# Why: no spring.datasource.* here. Docker Compose support (bootRun) and Testcontainers'
# @ServiceConnection (tests) supply the connection details, so no credentials live in config.
spring:
  application:
    name: inventory
```

**Spring: connection details.** Normally you'd configure a database like this:

```yaml
spring:
  datasource:
    url: jdbc:postgresql://localhost:5432/inventory
    username: inventory
    password: inventory
```

Behind the scenes, Spring turns those properties into a `JdbcConnectionDetails` object, and the connection pool is built from that object. Docker Compose support (on `bootRun`) and Testcontainers (in tests) **create that object directly** from the running container, and it takes priority over any `spring.datasource.*` properties. So the database is wherever the container happens to be, on whatever random port it got.

**Why nothing is written here:**
- **No hard-coded port**, so a random port just works.
- **No password in a committed file.**
- **Production is covered too.** There you'd set environment variables such as `SPRING_DATASOURCE_URL`, `SPRING_DATASOURCE_USERNAME` and `SPRING_DATASOURCE_PASSWORD`. Spring maps environment variables onto properties automatically ("relaxed binding": uppercase, with `_` instead of `.`), so this file never has to change.

**`spring.application.name: inventory`** shows up in every log line, as the `--- [inventory]` part, and identifies the service to tools such as monitoring.

**YAML vs `.properties`:** they're equivalent. `spring.application.name=inventory` would do the same thing. YAML groups nested keys, which reads better as settings accumulate.

**Check your understanding:** We deploy this app to a server with an existing Postgres at `db.example.com`. There's no Docker Compose there, and `spring-boot-docker-compose` isn't even in the jar. How do you point the app at that database **without editing any file in the repo**?

<ide_opened_file>The user opened the file c:\Users\rober\Documents\Projects\Nuuly_Inventory_Assessment\src\main\resources\application.yml in the IDE. This may or may not be related to the current task.</ide_opened_file>
Without editing any file? Wouldn't you need to update the application yaml with that database info?

You *could* do that, and it would work. But that means committing production database details (and probably the password) into the repo, and changing a file every time the environment changes. Spring gives you a better way.

**Spring doesn't read settings only from `application.yml`.** It checks several places in a fixed order, and anything higher up the list overrides anything lower:

```
1. Command-line arguments      java -jar inventory.jar --spring.datasource.url=...
2. Environment variables       SPRING_DATASOURCE_URL=...
3. application.yml             (inside the jar)
4. Spring Boot's defaults
```

`application.yml` is just one layer: the defaults that ship inside the jar. The server can put its own values on top without touching the jar. For `db.example.com`:

```powershell
$env:SPRING_DATASOURCE_URL      = "jdbc:postgresql://db.example.com:5432/inventory"
$env:SPRING_DATASOURCE_USERNAME = "inventory_app"
$env:SPRING_DATASOURCE_PASSWORD = "<from the server's secret store>"
java -jar inventory-0.0.1-SNAPSHOT.jar
```

**How environment variable names map:** Spring converts `SPRING_DATASOURCE_URL` into `spring.datasource.url` (uppercase to lowercase, `_` to `.`). This is called **relaxed binding**, and it exists because most shells don't allow dots in variable names.

**Why this matters beyond this project:** this is the standard way to deploy (it's rule III of the "twelve-factor app" guidelines). The *same jar* runs on your laptop, in test and in production, and only the environment differs. Passwords come from the server's secret store (Kubernetes secrets, AWS Secrets Manager, …) and never touch git. Expect to be asked about this in the interview.

**Try it yourself** (no database needed). The app name appears in every log line, so override it from outside:

```powershell
$env:SPRING_APPLICATION_NAME = "hello-override"
./gradlew bootRun
```

Every log line will say `[hello-override]` instead of `[inventory]`, even though `application.yml` still says `inventory`. Press Ctrl+C, then run `Remove-Item Env:SPRING_APPLICATION_NAME` to clean up.

So the env files are set at the infra level? They come in and the service reads and deals with them. Thats why you say we dont need to touch anything in the repo

Yes, exactly. One clarification on the wording: they're usually **environment variables**, not necessarily *files*. Every running process has a set of key/value pairs given to it by whatever launched it. In your terminal, `$env:X = ...` sets one for the programs you start from that terminal.

In a real deployment, whatever starts the service sets them:

| Where it runs | Where the variables are defined |
|---|---|
| Kubernetes | the Deployment manifest (`env:` section), with passwords pulled from a Kubernetes Secret |
| AWS ECS | the task definition, with secrets from AWS Secrets Manager |
| plain Docker | `docker run -e SPRING_DATASOURCE_URL=...` |
| a VM | a systemd unit file, or a startup script |

Those manifests belong to the infrastructure side. They often live in a separate infra/deploy repo, owned by whoever runs the platform. The service's side of the deal is simple: **read your configuration from the environment at startup**. Spring Boot does that for you automatically.

So the division of labor is:
- **The service repo** (ours) ships a jar with safe defaults, plus the list of settings it needs.
- **The infrastructure** says "in *this* environment, the database is here, and here's the password".

On *env files*: a `.env` file is a local-development shortcut for setting several variables at once, and some tools load one automatically. That's why our `.gitignore` already excludes `.env` and `.env.*`: they tend to hold real passwords and must never be committed.

When talking with Seth, Arctitect at Nuuly, he said they use spring over micronaut because dealing with different env variables for all different env levels was maddness. They were out of production because of a bug related to this for 3 days. 
Is my understanding of what he said sound right and associated with this? Is this a big benefit for spring over micronaut even though micronaut is much faster at start up?

Your understanding connects to what we just covered. But I can only tell you what's *plausible*, not what actually happened at Nuuly. Here's what I can say with confidence, and where I'd be guessing.

**How it connects.** Both frameworks do what we just discussed: config files inside the artifact, with environment variables layered on top. Micronaut has per-environment config (`application-{env}.yml`), and so does Spring (profiles). So it's not that Micronaut *can't* handle environment variables. The difference is in *how* each one resolves them, and those details are exactly where a production bug can hide.

**Known Micronaut behaviors that surprise teams used to Spring.** This is the speculative part: I don't know which, if any, bit Nuuly.
- **Automatic environment detection.** Micronaut guesses where it's running (Kubernetes, a cloud provider, a test) and turns on matching environments by itself. Config files for those environments then load without anyone asking for them. The same artifact can behave differently depending on where it lands.
- **Looser variable mapping.** Micronaut maps an environment variable like `FOO_BAR_BAZ` to *several* candidate property names (`foo.bar.baz`, `foo.bar-baz`, `foo-bar.baz`, …). That's more forgiving, but it can match a property you didn't intend.
- **Configuration settled at compile time.** Micronaut decides much of its wiring when the code is compiled, which is where its speed comes from. Some behavior that Spring decides at runtime is fixed earlier, which can confuse someone expecting Spring's behavior.

Any of these could plausibly cost three days: config bugs are hard to reproduce, because they depend on *where* the code runs, not on the code.

**Is this a big benefit for Spring, even though Micronaut starts faster?** For Nuuly's situation, it's a reasonable call:
- **Startup speed matters most** when instances start constantly: serverless functions, scaling from zero, short-lived jobs. A long-running service that starts a few times per deploy barely notices 2 seconds versus 6.
- **Predictability matters constantly.** A config bug that takes production down for 3 days costs more than all the startup time you'd ever save.
- **Spring's other advantages:** it's the most widely used JVM framework, so there's more documentation, more people who already know it, and more answered questions for every odd problem.
- **The speed gap has narrowed.** Spring now has ahead-of-time processing, GraalVM native images and CRaC (restoring an already-started JVM snapshot). You can adopt those for the services where startup matters.

**For the interview:** don't claim to know what the bug was. Show you understood the principle, and ask him. Something like: *"You mentioned environment config was the pain point with Micronaut. Was it the automatic environment detection, or how variables mapped to properties?"* Asking a specific question like that shows you understand how the configuration works, which is more convincing than repeating his story back to him.

Our README already says the speed gains "didn't outweigh the environment problems". Say if you want to add the three-day outage as supporting detail. It's your call, since it's Nuuly's internal story.

## 5. InventoryApplication.kt

**Role:** the entry point. `bootRun` or `java -jar` calls `main`, which starts Spring. Spring then finds and wires every controller, service and repository. No request ever passes through this file, but none could be served without it.

### The class

[InventoryApplication.kt:1-12](src/main/kotlin/com/robertwoolbright/inventory/InventoryApplication.kt#L1-L12)
```kotlin
// Study notes: docs/learning/notes/main/InventoryApplication.kt.md
package com.robertwoolbright.inventory

import org.springframework.boot.autoconfigure.SpringBootApplication
import org.springframework.boot.runApplication

/**
 * Entry point of the inventory service. Component scanning starts from this package, so every
 * controller, service and repository below it is picked up automatically.
 */
@SpringBootApplication
class InventoryApplication
```

**Spring: `@SpringBootApplication` is three annotations in one:**

| Annotation | Effect |
|---|---|
| `@SpringBootConfiguration` | This is a configuration class: it may declare beans, and it's what tests search for (file 7). |
| `@EnableAutoConfiguration` | Configure whatever the classpath implies: Web MVC is present, so start Tomcat; JDBC and the Postgres driver are present, so build a connection pool; and so on. |
| `@ComponentScan` | Find every `@Component`, `@Service`, `@Repository` and `@RestController` **in this package and below**, create one instance of each, and wire them together. |

**Why the file sits in the root package:** because of that scan. The future `com.robertwoolbright.inventory.inventory.InventoryController` is *below* this package, so Spring finds it automatically.

**Kotlin: a class with no body.** `class InventoryApplication`, with no `{}`. Kotlin lets you leave the braces off when there's nothing inside. Spring never calls anything on this class; it only reads its annotations. Java would need `public class InventoryApplication {}`.

**Kotlin: why `class` and not `object`?** Kotlin has `object` for singletons. But Spring wants to create configuration classes itself, and to subclass them (remember the proxies from the build file). # Walkthrough: project scaffold

  InventoryApplication.kt, support/TestcontainersConfiguration.kt, InventoryApplicationTests.kt

## Concepts covered

- Settings vs build file: settings decides *which* projects exist (`include(...)` for modules), build decides *how* each is built.
- Gradle Kotlin DSL is Kotlin: trailing lambdas, lambdas with receiver (type-safe builders), infix `version`, `=` on lazy properties.
- Final by default: Kotlin classes/methods are final; Spring proxies subclass and override, so `plugin.spring` opens them.
- Final is not immutable: `open`/`final` = subclassing; `val`/`var` = mutability.
- Dependency configurations: `implementation` vs `runtimeOnly` vs `developmentOnly`; compile vs runtime classpath.
- Platform types and `-Xjsr305=strict`: Java nullability annotations become real Kotlin types; a missed null check is a compile error.
- `param-property` annotation target: where `@Min(1)` on a constructor `val` lands (and why it could be silently ignored otherwise).
- Reified type parameters: `withType<Test>`, `runApplication<InventoryApplication>`.
- Docker Compose support: Spring starts the container, reads DB/user/password from compose.yaml and the port from Docker.
- Loopback port binding (`127.0.0.1::5432`) and why Docker's default is a security risk.
- Connection details: Compose and Testcontainers supply them, overriding `spring.datasource.*`.
- Property source precedence: command line > environment variables > application.yml > defaults; relaxed binding.
- Twelve-factor config: same jar everywhere, environment set by the infrastructure (k8s manifests, ECS task definitions).
- `@SpringBootApplication` = `@SpringBootConfiguration` + `@EnableAutoConfiguration` + `@ComponentScan`.
- Top-level functions (`InventoryApplicationKt`), importing a function, `Array<String>`, spread operator `*`.
- `@TestConfiguration` + `@Import`, `@ServiceConnection`, container lifecycle tied to the Spring context, context caching, Ryuk.
- `@SpringBootTest` finds `@SpringBootConfiguration` by searching up packages; smoke test vs slices.

- Q: Wouldn't you need to update application.yml with the production database info?
  A: No. Spring layers property sources; environment variables (set by the infrastructure) override
  application.yml, so the repo never holds environment-specific values or passwords.
- Q: So environment variables are set at the infrastructure level and the service just reads them?
  A: Yes. Whatever launches the process sets them (k8s Deployment + Secret, ECS task definition,
  `docker run -e`, systemd). `.env` files are a local convenience and are gitignored.
- Q: Seth (Nuuly architect) said they chose Spring over Micronaut because environment-variable
  handling across environments was painful and a related bug kept them out of production for
  3 days. Does that relate, and is it a real advantage despite Micronaut's faster startup?
  A: It relates directly to config layering. Possible Micronaut culprits (speculative): automatic
  environment detection, looser env-var-to-property mapping, compile-time decisions. Startup speed
  matters most for serverless/scale-from-zero; predictability matters constantly. Suggested asking
  Seth which mechanism it was rather than claiming to know.

  Java was installed, so its terminals have a stale environment. Fix: restart VS Code fully.

  fails to *compile* (not on the compile classpath); `runtimeOnly` enforces the java.sql-only design.

  it's only a warning; showed `?.` and `?:`.

  Mostly right; the port comes from Docker, not the file.

  precedence and relaxed binding; added to the application.yml notes. Follow-up
  (CLI vs env vs yml) → "cli-wins", correct.
- Controller in sibling package `com.robertwoolbright.web`? → "won't be found". Correct; added that the
  symptom is a silent 404 with no startup error.
- Who starts/stops the test container? → Spring, on bean creation / context close. Correct; added that
  with caching that means end of test run, and Ryuk as a safety net.
- Why keep `contextLoads`? → startup issues: dependencies, config, migrations. Correct; added that
  slices never assemble the full app.

## Follow-ups

- Restart VS Code so terminals see JAVA_HOME and Docker, then try the experiments:
  `docker ps` during bootRun; `$env:SPRING_APPLICATION_NAME = "hello-override"`; comment out
  `@Import` in InventoryApplicationTests and predict the failure.
- `?.` and `?:` were previewed only; cover properly when they first appear in real code.
- Optional: add Seth's Micronaut outage story to the README decision record (Robert's call).

  environment detection, looser env-var-to-property mapping, compile-time decisions. Startup speed
  matters most for serverless/scale-from-zero; predictability matters constantly. Suggested asking
  Seth which mechanism it was rather than claiming to know.
- (Environment) `./gradlew bootRun` failed with "JAVA_HOME is not set": VS Code was opened before
  Java was installed, so its terminals have a stale environment. Fix: restart VS Code fully.

## Understanding checks

- Splitting into modules: which file changes? → settings.gradle.kts with `include(...)`. Correct.
- Remove `plugin.spring`, add `@Transactional`: what breaks? → Correct on final vs open, but said a
  final class is "immutable". Clarified final ≠ immutable, that proxies wrap method calls, and that a
  final *method* fails silently. Added to the build notes.
- `import org.postgresql.PGConnection` with `runtimeOnly`? → "a dependency issue". Sharpened: it
  fails to *compile* (not on the compile classpath); `runtimeOnly` enforces the java.sql-only design.
- `@Nullable` + `result.length` with and without `-Xjsr305=strict`? → Correct. Added: without the flag
  it's only a warning; showed `?.` and `?:`.
- How does bootRun know the DB without application.yml settings? → "it's all in compose.yaml".
  Mostly right; the port comes from Docker, not the file.
- Deploy to db.example.com without editing files? → Unsure. Re-explained with property source
  precedence and relaxed binding; added to the application.yml notes. Follow-up
  (CLI vs env vs yml) → "cli-wins", correct.
- Controller in sibling package `com.robertwoolbright.web`? → "won't be found". Correct; added that the
  symptom is a silent 404 with no startup error.
- Who starts/stops the test container? → Spring, on bean creation / context close. Correct; added that
  with caching that means end of test run, and Ryuk as a safety net.
- Why keep `contextLoads`? → startup issues: dependencies, config, migrations. Correct; added that
  slices never assemble the full app.

## Follow-ups

- Restart VS Code so terminals see JAVA_HOME and Docker, then try the experiments:
  `docker ps` during bootRun; `$env:SPRING_APPLICATION_NAME = "hello-override"`; comment out
  `@Import` in InventoryApplicationTests and predict the failure.
- `?.` and `?:` were previewed only; cover properly when they first appear in real code.
- Optional: add Seth's Micronaut outage story to the README decision record (Robert's call).
